metadata.title: Timing of platelet-rich plasma administration in arthroscopic rotator cuff repair: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated as a biologic adjunct in arthroscopic rotator cuff repair (ARCR), yet clinical evidence remains heterogeneous. One potential source of variability is the timing of PRP administration, which may influence tendon-to-bone healing. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of PRP augmentation on structural healing and clinical outcomes following ARCR, with particular evaluation of outcomes according to the timing of PRP administration. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and registered on PROSPERO. PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane CENTRAL and Web of Science were searched through 19 February 2026. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing PRP augmentation with control in adult patients undergoing ARCR were included. Trials were stratified by timing of PRP administration (intraoperative, post-operative-only or combined). The primary outcome was retears assessed by post-operative imaging at ≥6 months. Pooled risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2 statistics. RESULTS: Fifteen RCTs (1214 patients; 647 PRP and 567 control) met inclusion criteria. Overall, PRP administration at ≥6 months was associated with a reduced risk of retears (RR, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.40-0.70; p < 0.001; I2 = 0%). Subgroup analysis demonstrated that intraoperative PRP significantly reduced retear rates at ≥6 months (RR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.35-0.68; p < 0.001; I2 = 0%) and ≥12 months (RR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.30-0.91; p = 0.021; I2 = 0%). Post-operative-only PRP did not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in retears (RR, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.01-8.12; p = 0.54). Absolute risk reduction at ≥6 months was approximately 12%, corresponding to a number needed to treat of 8. Functional outcome scores improved in both PRP and control groups, with significant differences between groups in included studies, but pooled analyses did not demonstrate consistent between-group differences. PRP was not associated with increased complication rates. CONCLUSION: Intraoperative PRP augmentation during ARCR is associated with a statistically significant reduction in retears. The limited post-operative-only PRP protocols do not demonstrate a comparable benefit and preclude a definitive conclusion that efficacy differs according to timing. These findings suggest a potential timing-dependent structural effect of PRP. However, structural improvements did not consistently translate into superior functional outcomes. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I.

metadata.title: Quadriceps and hamstring tendon autografts show similar clinical outcomes but distinct strength-recovery profiles after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A meta-analysis.
metadata.abstract: IMPORTANCE: Graft choice remains a central controversy in primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). Quadriceps tendon (QT) and hamstring tendon (HT) autografts may provided similar clinical outcomes but differ in donor-site morbidity and postoperative strength recovery. OBJECTIVE: To determine whether QT and HT autografts differ in patient-reported outcomes, knee stability, functional performance, strength recovery, donor-site morbidity, and safety after primary ACLR. EVIDENCE REVIEW: PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Embase were searched from inception to March 17, 2026, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) directly comparing QT and HT autografts. The protocol was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; CRD420261340928). Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using risk ratios (RRs) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MDs) or standardized mean differences (SMDs) for continuous outcomes, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. No external funding was received. FINDINGS: Fifteen RCTs involving 936 participants were included, with 470 participants receiving QT autografts and 466 receiving HT autografts. Mean ages ranged from 18.7 to 32.7 years, and most studies reported follow-up at 12 or 24 months. At 24 months, no statistically significant differences were detected between QT and HT autografts in IKDC score (MD = -1.19; 95% CI, -3.84 to 1.47; p = 0.38), Lysholm score (MD = 1.42; 95% CI, -0.60 to 3.45; p = 0.17), or Tegner score (MD = -0.15; 95% CI, -0.70 to 0.39; p = 0.58). At the final available follow-up, graft failure occurred in 12 of 265 participants (4.5%) in the QT group and 11 of 261 participants (4.2%) in the HT group, without a statistically significant difference (RR = 1.11; 95% CI, 0.49 to 2.48; p = 0.81). Overall adverse events also showed no statistically significant difference (RR = 0.71; 95% CI, 0.45 to 1.11; p = 0.13). QT autografts were associated with lower donor-site morbidity scores at 24 months (MD = -4.62; 95% CI, -9.21 to -0.03; p = 0.048), although this secondary finding was based on two trials. Knee stability, range of motion, return-to-sport, and hop-test outcomes showed no consistent differences. At 12 months, HT autografts were associated with relatively greater quadriceps strength symmetry, whereas QT autografts were associated with relatively greater hamstring strength symmetry and higher hamstring-to-quadriceps (H/Q) strength ratios. - CONCLUSION AND RELEVANCE: QT and HT autografts produced similar patient-reported, stability, return-to-sport, and safety outcomes after primary ACLR but demonstrated distinct graft-specific strength-recovery profiles. These findings support individualized graft selection rather than consistent clinical superiority of either graft. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, systematic review, and meta-analysis of RCTs.

metadata.title: Effects of Combined Blood Flow Restriction and Neuromuscular Electrical Stimulation Versus Blood Flow Restriction Alone: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
metadata.abstract: Background/Objectives: Blood flow restriction (BFR) training is increasingly combined with neuromuscular electrical stimulation (NMES) in musculoskeletal rehabilitation to augment strength and hypertrophy, but whether NMES adds benefit beyond BFR alone remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis compared combined BFR + NMES with BFR alone for muscle strength, muscle morphology (mass, thickness, cross-sectional area), neuromuscular activation, and functional performance. Methods: Randomized trials comparing simultaneous BFR + NMES with BFR alone were eligible. MEDLINE via PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Google Scholar were searched from inception through 15 September 2026. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data; risk of bias was assessed with Cochrane RoB 2 and certainty with GRADE. Random-effects meta-analysis was restricted to independent parallel-group comparisons; crossover and limb-randomized results were pooled only when paired effect estimates and variances were available, otherwise synthesized narratively. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251076162). Results: Five randomized trials involving 174 participants were included. The studies represented healthy-participant training, experimental limb disuse, acute physiological responses, and low-load training in football players with knee osteoarthritis. Quantitative synthesis of torque-based strength found no clear difference between BFR + NMES and BFR alone (MD -41.78 Nm, 95% CI -396.68 to 313.12; p = 0.375; 2 trials, 52 participants), with substantial statistical heterogeneity. Cross-sectional area and rectus femoris EMG RMS were each reported by only two trials and were synthesized narratively. Certainty of evidence was very low across all outcomes. Conclusions: Current evidence does not establish a consistent additional benefit of adding NMES to BFR. The pooled torque-based estimate is exploratory because of the small evidence base, substantial statistical heterogeneity, imprecision, and differences in clinical context and outcome measurement. A possible effect on preserving muscle mass during short-term experimental disuse remains preliminary. None of the included trials directly investigated BFR + NMES following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), and its effectiveness in this population remains undetermined.

metadata.title: Effectiveness of Digital Health Interventions on Rehabilitation Outcomes in Patients After Total Knee Arthroplasty: Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) is the most effective treatment for end-stage knee osteoarthritis, but some patients continue to experience persistent postoperative pain, stiffness, and impaired functional recovery. Digital health interventions are increasingly used in rehabilitation after TKA, but their comparative effectiveness remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of different digital health interventions on rehabilitation outcomes in patients after TKA and to compare and rank these interventions in terms of pain relief, active knee flexion range of motion (ROM), and knee function to provide evidence for selecting optimal rehabilitation strategies. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Google Scholar, Scopus, CINAHL, MEDLINE (via OvidSP), CNKI, Wanfang, and VIP to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) meeting the inclusion criteria. The RoB 2 tool (Risk of Bias 2; Cochrane) was used to assess risk of bias, and the confidence in network meta-analysis (CINeMA) framework was used to evaluate certainty of evidence. Traditional meta-analysis and network meta-analysis (NMA) were performed using Stata (version 17.0; StataCorp LLC). A random-effects model (DerSimonian-Laird method for estimating τ²) was consistently used across all analyses. For outcomes measured with the same or convertible scales, mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs were used to pool effect sizes. Surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) values were calculated to summarize the ranking probabilities. RESULTS: A total of 36 RCTs involving 3067 patients after TKA were included. NMA results showed that compared with conventional rehabilitation (CR), for active flexion ROM, rehabilitation robot (RR; MD 8.96, 95% CI 5.86-12.05), mobile app-based telerehabilitation (MAT; MD 6.36, 95% CI 2.81-9.91), and virtual reality (VR; MD 5.92, 95% CI 2.94-8.90) were significantly superior to CR; for the Hospital for Special Surgery knee score, VR (MD 9.53, 95% CI 5.18-13.88), intelligent rehabilitation system-based telerehabilitation (MD 6.90, 95% CI 2.35-11.44), and RR (MD 5.32, 95% CI 1.61-9.04) were significantly superior to CR; for pain, RR and MAT had relatively high ranking probabilities, but the 95% CIs of most comparisons included 0; for the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index and Timed Up and Go test, only internet videoconference-based telerehabilitation and VR-based telerehabilitation, respectively, were significantly superior to CR. The certainty of evidence for most comparisons was low or very low. CONCLUSIONS: Digital health interventions may improve pain, active knee flexion ROM, and knee function in patients after TKA. In the SUCRA ranking, RR, VR, and MAT showed favorable ranking probabilities; however, because the network was predominantly star-shaped and the rankings were derived largely from indirect comparisons, these findings should be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive. Further high-quality studies with direct head-to-head comparisons are needed.

metadata.title: Neurocognitive Alterations Manifested as Reaction Time Deficits Following ACL Reconstruction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Observational Studies.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) is associated with changes in cognitive-motor processing that may persist beyond physical recovery and are not fully identified by conventional physical performance assessments. OBJECTIVE: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate neurocognitive function as expressed through cognitive-motor performance following ACLR compared with healthy individuals, with particular emphasis on reaction time and higher-order cognitive outcomes. METHODS: Four databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, Embase) were searched from inception to December 2025. Eligibility criteria included observational studies on cognitive-motor outcomes in individuals from ACLR recovery and healthy controls. Data extraction followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Methodological quality was evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute appraisal tools. Random-effects models were used to calculate standardized mean differences with 95% confidence intervals. Heterogeneity was assessed with I2, subgroup analyses and publication bias evaluations. RESULTS: Twenty-one non-randomised studies involving 986 participants Twenty-one non-randomised studies involving 986 participantswere included. Neurocognitive performance showed a significant impairment in reaction time from ACLR recovery with a moderate effect size (standardized mean difference = 0.56, 95% confidence interval 0.41-0.71, p < 0.001) and high heterogeneity (I2 = 78%). In contrast, pooled analyses showed no statistically significant differences for error rate, accuracy, visual memory, or visual motor speed. CONCLUSIONS: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction is associated with persistent reaction time deficits, whereas pooled analyses of error rate, accuracy, visual memory, and visual motor speed did not demonstrate statistically significant differences compared with healthy controls. This pattern suggests selective impairment in the temporal efficiency of cognitive-motor processing rather than generalized cognitive dysfunction. Reaction time may represent a potential marker of altered cognitive-motor processing following ACLR; however, prospective studies are needed to determine its prognostic value and clinical utility for post-ACLR assessment and return-to-sport decision making.

metadata.title: Interval Between Injury and Surgery Influences Knee Biomechanics During Walking in Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstructed Patients: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) is commonly performed to restore anatomical and functional knee stability. Although altered walking biomechanics have been observed post-ACLR, previous studies have not consistently accounted for the interval between injury and surgery. OBJECTIVE: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine whether walking-related knee biomechanical alterations following ACLR are transient or persist over time, and whether the timing of surgery influences these alterations. METHODS: Five electronic databases (Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, Physiotherapy Evidence Database [PEDro], and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials [CENTRAL]) were systematically searched from inception through August 2026. Studies comparing walking biomechanics between patients who underwent ACLR and healthy controls and reporting the interval between anterior cruciate ligament injury and reconstructive surgery were included. Biomechanical outcomes during the stance phase of walking were extracted and stratified according to the interval between injury and surgery: short term (0 to < 6 months), mid-term (6 to < 12 months), and long term (≥ 12 months). Standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals were calculated using a random-effects model. Study quality was assessed using a modified Downs and Black checklist. RESULTS: Of the 3522 identified records, 16 studies involving male and female participants aged 18-55 years met the inclusion criteria. The mean methodological quality score was 65%, indicating an overall moderate level of methodological quality. Compared with healthy controls, ACLR participants demonstrated lower peak knee flexion angle (SMD = - 0.33, 95% confidence interval [CI] - 0.64 to - 0.02, p = 0.03, I2 = 57%), peak knee adduction angle (SMD = - 0.47, 95% CI - 0.92 to - 0.01, p = 0.04, I2 = 66%), and peak knee flexion moment (SMD = - 0.64, 95% CI - 1.05 to - 0.23, p = 0.002, I2 = 76%). In subgroup analyses, the long-term group (≥ 12 months between injury and surgery) demonstrated lower peak knee flexion angle (SMD = - 0.27, 95% CI - 0.54 to - 0.00, p = 0.05, I2 = 8%) and peak knee flexion moment (SMD = - 1.97, 95% CI - 3.77 to - 0.17, p = 0.03, I2 = 88%). The short-term group (0 to < 6 months) demonstrated lower peak knee adduction angle (SMD = - 0.79, 95% CI - 1.18 to - 0.40, p < 0.0001, I2 = 19%) and peak knee extension moment (SMD = - 0.55, 95% CI - 0.93 to - 0.18, p = 0.004, I2 = 50%). CONCLUSIONS: The interval between anterior cruciate ligament injury and ACLR was associated with differences in postoperative walking biomechanics. Delayed reconstruction (≥ 12 months) is associated with persistent sagittal plane deficits, which may reflect chronic neuromuscular adaptations or preoperative joint degeneration. In contrast, early surgery (within 6 months after anterior cruciate ligament injury) was associated with fewer long-term sagittal-plane deficits, although temporary frontal-plane asymmetries and extension deficits may persist during the early postoperative period and may improve with rehabilitation. These findings underscore the importance of considering the timing of ACLR when planning surgery and postoperative rehabilitation to support walking recovery.

metadata.title: The role of scapular muscles strengthening in lateral epicondylalgia rehabilitation: A systematic review with meta-analysis.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Lateral epicondylalgia is a prevalent tendinopathy often recurring despite conventional physiotherapy. Emerging evidence suggests that scapular muscles strengthening improves outcomes by addressing proximal kinetic chain deficits. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the effectiveness of scapular muscles strengthening combined with conventional physiotherapy compared with conventional physiotherapy alone in patients with Lateral epicondylalgia. STUDY DESIGN: Systematic review with meta-analysis. METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, PEDro, Scopus, Web of Science and ScienceDirect were searched up to January 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized experimental studies with Lateral Epicondylalgia were included. Outcomes were pain (Visual Analog Scale, Numeric Pain Rating Scale), grip strength (dynamometer), and function {pain and disability (Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation)}. Methodological quality was assessed using Physiotherapy Evidence Database (PEDro) scale and Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) appraisal tool. Risk of bias was evaluated using Revised Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool for Randomized Trials and Risk of Bias in Non-Randomized Studies of interventions, and certainty of evidence using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. RESULTS: Twelve studies [10 RCTs, 2 non-randomized) were included, with 8 RCTs pooled for meta-analysis. Scapular muscles strengthening plus conventional therapy demonstrated significant functional improvement (PRTEE: MD = -9.33; 95% CI -15.01 to -3.65; p = 0.001; I² = 73%). No significant pooled effect was found for pain (SMD = -0.36; 95% CI -1.24-0.52; p = 0.43; I² = 86%) or grip strength (SMD = 0.19; 95% CI -0.09-0.47; p = 0.18). Overall low to moderate risk of bias, with good RCTs quality (PEDro mean score=6/10) and high non- RCTs quality (JBI). Overall certainty of evidence was moderate for pain and grip strength and low for PRTEE. CONCLUSION: Scapular muscles strengthening combined with conventional physiotherapy provides superior functional outcomes compared with conventional therapy alone in patients with LE. Effects on pain and grip strength remain inconclusive.

metadata.title: Network meta-analysis of the efficacy of different exercise therapies in patients with knee osteoarthritis.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) is a leading cause of disability in the elderly and a growing social burden due to aging and increasing obesity rates. This study aims to investigate the effects of different exercise modalities on pain, physical function, stiffness, and muscle strength in patients with KOA. METHODS: A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and EBSCO databases for randomized controlled trials evaluating the efficacy of exercise therapy for KOA from January 2000 to 16 August 2025, followed by an updated search through 28 March 2026. No additional eligible studies were identified in the updated search. In total, 51 studies involving 3,045 participants (71.7% female; study-group mean ages ranged from 50.3 to 74.4 years) were included. The studies were conducted in 14 countries across Asia, Europe, North America, South America, and Oceania. A network meta-analysis was performed using Stata 16.0. This systematic review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251177632). RESULTS: The results showed that mind-body exercise was the most effective in reducing pain (standardized mean differences (SMD) = -1.13, 95% confidence interval (CI) [-1.47 to -0.79], P < 0.001, Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking Curve (SUCRA) = 83%) and improving joint stiffness (SMD = -1.15, 95% CI [-1.59 to -0.70], P < 0.001, SUCRA = 78.5%). Mixed exercise ranked highest in improving knee function (SMD = -1.43, 95% CI [-2.31 to -0.55], P < 0.001, SUCRA = 81.8%), followed by mind-body exercise (SMD = -1.28, 95% CI [-1.64 to -0.93], P < 0.001, SUCRA = 77.4%). Strength training was most effective in enhancing muscle strength (SMD = 0.79, 95% CI [0.470-1.12], P < 0.001, SUCRA = 79.1%). CONCLUSION: Mind-body exercise appeared to be the most favorable option for reducing pain and stiffness in patients with knee osteoarthritis, whereas strength training appeared to be the most beneficial for improving muscle strength. These findings may help inform individualized exercise prescription, but should be interpreted cautiously given the uncertainty and limitations of the available evidence.

metadata.title: Effects of caffeine supplementation on exercise-induced muscle damage: A systematic review.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) commonly occurs following unaccustomed or high-intensity exercise and is characterized by delayed-onset muscle soreness, elevated muscle damage biomarkers, and transient declines in muscle function. Caffeine, a widely consumed ergogenic aid, has been proposed to mitigate these adverse effects; however, the evidence across studies remains equivocal. This systematic review aimed to synthesize findings from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the effects of caffeine supplementation on markers of EIMD. METHODS: Following preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses guidelines, a comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar databases, supplemented by citation tracking. RCTs published between 2005 and 2025 that included human participants and reported direct or indirect indicators of EIMD were eligible. Fifteen RCTs (n = 222) were included and assessed for methodological quality using the PEDro scale. RESULTS: Caffeine doses ranged from 3 to 6 mg/kg. Among the 6 studies assessing delayed-onset muscle soreness, 4 reported significant reductions in perceived soreness within 24 to 48 hours post-exercise, whereas 2 found no effect or adverse responses. Eleven studies examined biochemical markers; most detected no significant differences between caffeine and placebo, while 2 observed higher creatine kinase levels in the caffeine group. Five studies evaluated functional performance; some indicated attenuation of decrements in maximal voluntary isometric contraction or isokinetic torque, although results were inconsistent. CONCLUSION: Caffeine supplementation may transiently reduce subjective muscle soreness and, under certain conditions, help preserve muscle function following EIMD, but its effects on biochemical markers are inconsistent. The overall efficacy appears to depend on factors such as exercise modality, dosage, timing, and inter-individual variability. Larger, well-controlled RCTs with standardized protocols are needed to clarify caffeine's role in muscle damage and recovery.

metadata.title: Efficacy and safety study of diclofenac epolamine topical patch in accelerating rehabilitation of moderate hamstring strain: A randomized controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Moderate hamstring strain is a common sports injury impairing daily and athletic function. While topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) offer localized pain relief with reduced systemic effects, high-quality evidence specific to hamstring injury is limited. OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the effect of a short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch combined with rehabilitation on pain and functional recovery in moderate hamstring strain. METHODS: In this single-center, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 120 patients were randomized to an experimental group (diclofenac patch twice daily for 14 days plus rehabilitation) or a control group (placebo patch plus identical rehabilitation). Outcomes assessed included pain measured by the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), as the primary endpoint, muscle strength, knee range of motion (ROM), functional back-kick test, time to rehabilitation criteria and safety (adverse events, liver/renal function). RESULTS: The diclofenac group demonstrated significantly greater pain reduction at days 14, 21 and 28 post-intervention (all p < 0.01). Muscle strength recovery was superior at days 21 and 28, knee ROM improved more at day 28 and functional back-kick performance was better at day 28 (all p < 0.05). Time to meet rehabilitation criteria was significantly shorter in the experimental group (p = 0.002). Adverse event incidence and changes in liver/renal function were similar between groups (all p > 0.05). CONCLUSION: A short-course topical diclofenac epolamine patch, combined with rehabilitation training, effectively alleviates pain, accelerates functional recovery, and is safe for treating moderate hamstring strain, supporting its use in clinical and sports rehabilitation.

metadata.title: Selective recovery effects of short-term beetroot juice supplementation after exercise-induced muscle damage in trained female volleyball players.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Beetroot juice (BRJ) has been proposed as a nutritional aid for recovery from exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD), but evidence in female team-sport athletes is limited. It also remains unclear whether any benefit extends across functional, pain-related, swelling, and strength outcomes. METHODS: Seventeen female university volleyball players entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Four did not complete the second period, so outcomes were analyzed with linear mixed models. After baseline testing, participants performed 200 loaded vertical jumps and consumed BRJ or placebo at 24, 48, and 72 h post-EIMD. Recovery outcomes were countermovement jump (CMJ) height, volleyball-specific agility time, pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, visual analog scale soreness, and knee isokinetic measures. Holm-adjusted planned contrasts were used. RESULTS: CMJ height was the clearest BRJ-related functional finding. The treatment × time interaction showed a trend toward statistical significance (P = 0.062), and CMJ height was higher under BRJ than PLA at 72 h post-EIMD (P = 0.033, d = 1.01). Calf pressure pain threshold also favored BRJ at 72 h, accompanied by a significant treatment × time interaction (P < 0.001). In contrast, agility time and soreness changed over time without clear between-condition differences, while thigh pressure pain threshold, thigh circumference, and low-velocity knee isokinetic outcomes showed no consistent BRJ-related advantage. CONCLUSIONS: Short-term BRJ supplementation was associated with selective rather than generalized recovery benefits after EIMD in trained female volleyball players. The clearest findings were higher CMJ height and calf PPT under BRJ than PLA at 72 h, whereas the remaining outcomes showed no consistent treatment-related differences.

metadata.title: Maximal Aerobic Capacity and Aging in Female Masters Athletes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Maximal aerobic capacity ( V ˙ O2max) represents the highest rate at which the body can use oxygen during intense exercise and is a key determinant of endurance performance. Although age-related declines in V ˙ O2max have been well documented in male individuals, less is known about this trajectory in female Masters athletes, defined as individuals aged 40 years or older who often engage in lifelong endurance training. OBJECTIVE: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to quantify cross-sectional age-related differences in directly measured V ˙ O2max among female Masters endurance athletes. METHODS: PubMed and Web of Science were searched from database inception to 14 May, 2025 for studies reporting directly measured V ˙ O2max in female Masters endurance athletes aged 40 years or older. Eligible exercise modalities included running, cycling, swimming, and large muscle-mass ergometry, with testing conducted under standard environmental conditions. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using a modified Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Pooled mean V ˙ O2max values were calculated for predefined age groups (40-49, 50-59, 60-69, and 70 years or older) using a random-effects meta-analysis. Meta-regression was used to estimate the relationship between age and V ˙ O2max. RESULTS: Sixty-nine studies, including 1903 female Masters athletes, met the inclusion criteria. Pooled mean relative V ˙ O2max was 45 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% confidence interval [CI] 43.0-46.8) in athletes aged 40-49 years, 40 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI 38.5-41.7) in those aged 50-59 years, 35 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI 33.2-37.1) in those aged 60-69 years, and 30 mL·kg-1·min-1 (95% CI 27.2-31.8) in athletes aged 70 years or older. Meta-regression demonstrated that each additional year of age was associated with a 0.57 mL·kg-1·min-1 lower V ˙ O2max (95% CI - 0.70 to - 0.44; P < 0.0001), equivalent to about 11.7% per decade. The association was consistent across testing modalities. CONCLUSIONS: This systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrates a progressive age-related decrease in directly measured V ˙ O2max among female Masters endurance athletes. Maximal aerobic capacity declines at an average rate of 0.57 mL·kg-1·min-1 per year after age 40 years, corresponding to approximately 11.7% per decade. This decline is evident across endurance sport disciplines and appears consistent with physiological changes associated with aging despite sustained endurance training. These findings provide female-specific reference values and a quantitative framework for future studies on aerobic capacity trajectories in female athletes. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: The protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/S2RXZ ).

metadata.title: Effectiveness of Adding Neuromuscular Training to Conventional Physiotherapy in Adults with Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
metadata.abstract: Background/Objectives: Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) is associated with pain, functional limitation and impaired balance. This study investigated whether adding neuromuscular training to conventional physiotherapy provides additional benefit over conventional physiotherapy alone in adults with PFPS. Methods: In this single-blind randomized controlled trial (NCT06407414), 56 adults aged 30-60 years with PFPS were randomized to conventional physiotherapy alone (control) or conventional physiotherapy plus neuromuscular training, each performed three times per week for 12 weeks as a home-based program with physiotherapist follow-up every three weeks. The analysis was per protocol and included the 50 of 56 randomized participants (25 per group) who completed the trial. The primary outcome was the Kujala Patellofemoral Score. Secondary outcomes were pain (Visual Analog Scale, VAS), the 30-Second Chair Stand Test, the Y Balance Test, the International Physical Activity Questionnaire-Short Form (IPAQ) and, as an exploratory outcome, the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Results: After treatment, the neuromuscular training group had higher Kujala scores (median 77 vs. 65; r = 0.81, 95% CI 0.69-0.89) and lower VAS scores (r = 0.72, 95% CI 0.55-0.83), and performed better on the chair stand test (mean difference 2.60 repetitions, 95% CI 0.88-4.32) and IPAQ-walking; these differences remained significant after Bonferroni correction for 12 comparisons, although for the chair stand test this was not consistent in a supplementary change-score analysis. Y Balance Test values are reported descriptively only, because the groups differed at baseline and the analytical definition of the reported values (stance limb) could not be verified against the original records. Between-group differences in the other IPAQ domains and the PSQI were not significant and were inconclusive. Conclusions: Under the conditions of this trial, adding neuromuscular training to conventional physiotherapy produced greater short-term improvements in pain and function than conventional physiotherapy alone. No conclusion is drawn regarding dynamic balance, and the effect on sleep quality remains uncertain.

metadata.title: Effect of Excision of the Infrapatellar Fat Pad in Total Knee Arthroplasty: A Double-Blinded Randomized Controlled Trial.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: The infrapatellar (Hoffa's) fat pad is frequently excised during total knee arthroplasty (TKA) to improve exposure, but its role in postoperative pain and function is uncertain. Previous randomized trials and meta-analyses are equivocal, with follow-up limited to 12 months. METHODS: We conducted a single-center, participant- and assessor-blinded, parallel-group randomized controlled trial. A total of 181 patients undergoing elective primary TKA for osteoarthritis were randomized intraoperatively to fat pad excision (removed) or minimal resection (retained). Implants and rehabilitation were standardized. The primary outcome was the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) at 24 months; the secondary outcome was the Oxford Knee Score (OKS) at three, 12, and 24 months. Groups were compared using Mann-Whitney U-tests, and within-group changes over time using Kruskal-Wallis tests. In total, 140 participants were analyzed at 24 months (74 removed, 66 retained; 22% loss to follow-up). RESULTS: Both groups improved significantly across all KOOS subscales and OKS over time (P-values < 0.05), with gains exceeding the minimal clinically important difference on KOOS Pain. There were no significant between-group differences in KOOS or OKS at any time point (P-values > 0.05). The only within-group gain unique to one arm was KOOS Symptoms in the removed group between three and 24 months (P-values < 0.05). The KOOS scores did not improve between 12 and 24 months. CONCLUSION: In this study, excision or preservation of the fat pad did not significantly influence pain or function at two years postoperatively. The absence of change beyond 12 months suggests future trials could shorten follow-up.

metadata.title: Prospective Polynomial Characterization of Tibial Plateau Geometry Shows No Association With Contralateral ACL Injury in Female Athletes.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are common in athletic people, with young female athletes at particularly high risk. After ACL injury, reconstruction, and return to sport, many sustain contralateral ACL (CACL) injuries. While tibial plateau cartilage surface geometry has been associated with first-time ACL injury risk, its role in subsequent CACL injury remains unclear. HYPOTHESIS: The normal knee of female athletes who suffered a first-time ACL injury, underwent reconstruction, returned to preinjury activities and subsequently suffered a CACL injury will have tibial plateau cartilage surface geometry that is different compared with an equivalent population who did not sustain a subsequent CACL injury. STUDY DESIGN: Prospective cohort study. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 2. METHODS: A total of 199 subjects who suffered a first-time ACL injury, had reconstruction, returned to preinjury activities and had a contralateral knee that was normal underwent bilateral magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan acquisitions. Tibial plateau cartilage geometry was assessed on the uninjured, normal knees using T1-weighted Fast Field Echo MRI. Parasagittal slices at maximum cartilage concavity in medial and lateral compartments of the tibia were characterized by fitting fifth-order polynomials. Female athletes who sustained a CACL injury within 4 years of reconstruction and return to sport (n = 12) were matched and compared with a group of female athletes who did not sustain CACL injury (n = 24). Random coefficient mixed-effects regression was used to assess group differences in polynomial functions. RESULTS: No significant differences in tibial cartilage surface geometry were found between the first-time ACL and first-time ACL + CACL injury groups in the medial (P = 0.23) and lateral (P = 0.18) compartments. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that characterization of tibial plateau cartilage geometry in the normal knee of subjects who underwent reconstruction after a first-time ACL injury is insufficient to predict who will on go on to suffer a subsequent CACL injury. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: More comprehensive predictive models incorporating anatomic, biomechanical, and psychological factors are likely needed to identify those at increased risk for CACL injury after a first-time ACL injury and reconstruction.

metadata.title: Effectiveness of a Structured Post-Platelet Rich Plasma Rehabilitation Approach on Pain and Function in Subacromial Pain Syndrome: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Subacromial pain syndrome (SAPS) causes pain and functional limitation. Platelet-Rich Plasma (PRP) is increasingly used as a supportive treatment. Optimal rehabilitation after PRP is unclear. This study investigated the effectiveness of a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach on pain and function. METHODS: Sixty participants with SAPS were randomized to two groups; 54 completed the study and were included in the final per-protocol analysis (27 per group). During a 21-day period, the study group received a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach in addition to standard conventional physiotherapy, while the control group received standard conventional physiotherapy alone. Range of motion, muscle strength, and posture were evaluated. In addition, outcome measures included the Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire (SF-MPQ), Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand Questionnaire (DASH), Functional Impairment Test-Hand and Neck/Shoulder/Arm (FIT-HaNSA) and Constant-Murley Shoulder Score, which were administered for assessment purposes. RESULTS: Corbin Posture Scale scores decreased in both groups (p < 0.05). Pain reduction was greater in the study group (VAS: from 9.00 ± 0.67 to 2.92 ± 1.14 versus from 9.11 ± 0.64 to 7.96 ± 0.75; SF-MPQ: from 27.07 ± 4.41 to 10.07 ± 3.33 versus from 21.33 ± 2.46 to 19.37 ± 2.35; p < 0.001). Improvements in Constant-Murley, DASH, and FIT-HaNSA scores, shoulder muscle strength, and active and passive range of motion were significantly greater in the study group (p < 0.001). DISCUSSION: Adding a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach to standard conventional physiotherapy may provide additional short-term improvements in pain, muscle strength, range of motion, and shoulder function compared with standard conventional physiotherapy alone in individuals with SAPS. However, long-term follow-up was not conducted. Therefore, the sustainability of the observed improvements remains unclear. Future studies should investigate the long-term effects of structured post-PRP rehabilitation approaches. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT07410208; registered on January 21, 2026.

metadata.title: Psychological interventions for anorexia nervosa in female athletes: A mixed-methods systematic review.
metadata.abstract: ObjectiveFemale athletes are at high risk of anorexia nervosa. Current clinical guidelines and psychological treatments are largely based on evidence from the general population, highlighting the need for a tailored review of the evidence. This review addresses two complementary questions: first, what evidence exists regarding the effectiveness of psychological interventions; and second, how do athletes with anorexia nervosa experience psychological treatment and recovery, and what factors may influence these experiences?MethodsA convergent, segregated mixed-methods systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines and the Joanna Briggs Institute guidelines (PROSPERO: CRD420251073240). Eight databases were searched up to April 2026. Studies were eligible if they involved adult female athletes aged ≥18 years, had a clinical diagnosis of anorexia nervosa and included a psychological intervention component. Quantitative findings were synthesised narratively using the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis framework, with certainty assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach. Qualitative findings underwent Joanna Briggs Institute meta-aggregation, with certainty assessed using the Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research approach. The findings were then integrated.ResultsEleven studies involving 153 participants (136 female and 17 male) were included. Most studies were conducted in the United States and used cognitive behavioural therapy as a core intervention. The certainty of evidence was very low across all quantitative outcomes (eating disorder psychopathology, weight restoration and return to sport), although the findings indicated potential for recovery. Qualitative evidence suggested that recovery is influenced by environmental, cultural and multidisciplinary support factors. Three themes illustrated these influences, and the integrated findings provided further insight.ConclusionStandard psychological treatments appear capable of supporting recovery in athletes, although outcomes may be enhanced when treatment delivery incorporates athlete-specific considerations, such as athletic identity, performance motivation, coach involvement and return-to-sport planning. Interventions may be more effective when they incorporate sport-specific cultural competence, performance-framed cognitive restructuring, structured coach involvement and return-to-sport goals. Future research should prioritise athlete-adapted experimental designs with sport-specific outcome measures to strengthen the evidence base.

metadata.title: Effects of Whey Protein Supplementation on Muscle Damage, Hepatic Stress, and Inflammatory Markers in Power- and Endurance-Trained Athletes.
metadata.abstract: This study investigated the effects of 8 weeks of whey protein supplementation (30 g/day) on biomarkers of liver function, inflammation, and muscle damage in trained power-trained (predominantly speed-power/anaerobic-power disciplines) and endurance-trained athletes, in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design. Fifty-nine male athletes were stratified into power (n = 30) and endurance (n = 29) groups, then randomly assigned to a whey protein group (WG) or a placebo control group (CG). Biomarkers assessed pre- and post-intervention included alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), C-reactive protein (CRP), and creatine kinase (CK). Significant reductions in ALT, AST, and CK were observed in both endurance- and power-trained athletes after supplementation (p = 0.001, p = 0.015, p = 0.001, and p = 0.003 respectively), indicating attenuated hepatic and muscular stress. Among the four biomarkers, only ALT displayed a statistically significant three-way interaction (Time × Supplementation × Training modality; p = 0.003), identifying it as the sole marker showing a genuine modality-specific differential response to supplementation. A significant within-group reduction in CRP was additionally observed in the supplemented power-trained athletes (p = 0.039), whereas endurance athletes showed only minor, non-significant changes; because the omnibus three-way interaction for CRP was not significant, this finding is reported as a within-group trend rather than evidence of a differential effect between modalities. Placebo groups demonstrated stable or increased enzyme and CRP values, particularly in endurance athletes. These findings suggest that whey protein may attenuate exercise-induced hepatic and muscular stress across training modalities, with a modality-specific effect on hepatic stress markers (ALT) observed in power-trained athletes. The results highlight whey protein's potential as a nutritional aid to promote recovery and physiological adaptation, possibly mediated by antioxidant and anti-inflammatory mechanisms. Further studies are warranted to examine long-term outcomes and dose-response effects across different training profiles.

metadata.title: Platelet Concentrates in Tooth Replantation: A Narrative Review and Evidence Synthesis of Periodontal and Pulpal Healing.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The prognosis of an avulsed, replanted tooth over the long term hinges on whether the periodontal ligament (PDL) and the dental pulp can be preserved or regenerated. When extra-oral dry time is prolonged, PDL necrosis follows, and the root becomes prone to inflammatory or replacement (ankylotic) resorption. Platelet concentrates-platelet-rich plasma (PRP), leukocyte- and platelet-rich plasma (L-PRP), and platelet-rich fibrin (PRF)-are autologous biomaterials that supply growth factors and may influence this healing process. This review asks whether autologous platelet concentrates reduce inflammatory and replacement (ankylotic) root resorption and improve periodontal and pulpal healing after delayed or intentional tooth replantation, compared with no adjunct, and whether residual periodontal ligament (PDL) viability changes this effect. MATERIAL AND METHODS: This narrative synthesis (not a systematic review) draws together recent controlled clinical and animal studies with the case-report and preclinical literature already captured in the only published systematic review on this topic. The search covered PubMed, Google Scholar, the Cochrane Library, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science, from January to May 2026. RESULTS: In preclinical models, L-PRP and PRF promote pulpal repair, tertiary dentin formation, and attenuated inflammatory root resorption, although neither consistently prevents ankylosis once PDL viability has been lost. In one retrospective comparative study of intentional replantation in hopeless teeth, PRF combined with root-surface biomodification produced greater clinical attachment gain and a larger reduction in probing depth than replantation alone, a direction consistent with earlier case reports. Small, largely non-randomized samples and unstandardized protocols still limit this evidence. CONCLUSIONS: Platelet concentrates are biologically plausible adjuncts that improve periodontal and pulpal healing indices, yet they do not reliably prevent ankylosis. Their clinical role will remain undefined until prospective randomized trials with standardized protocols are available.

metadata.title: Five-year outcomes after brace-free versus brace-based rehabilitation following isolated anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with hamstring tendon autograft: long-term follow-up of a randomized controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Postoperative knee bracing following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) remains common practice despite growing evidence questioning its clinical benefit. Previous studies demonstrated that brace-free rehabilitation was noninferior to brace-based rehabilitation one year after isolated ACLR using hamstring tendon autograft; however, its long-term effects remain unknown. The purpose of this study was to evaluate long-term effects five years after surgery. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Patients enrolled in a prospective randomized controlled trial conducted between 2016 and 2019 were recontacted approximately five years after isolated primary ACLR with hamstring tendon autograft for a long-term follow-up. In the original trial, 139 patients had been randomized to postoperative rehabilitation without a brace (n = 71) or with a functional knee brace (n = 68). Participants completed several patient-reported outcome measures. Furthermore, a standardized telephone interview was performed. Changes between the one-year and five-year follow-up were analyzed. RESULTS: Ninety-seven patients participated in the long-term follow-up (n = 45 brace-free group, n = 52 brace group). Mean follow-up was 5.2 ± 1.0 years. No significant differences were observed between groups regarding subjective knee function, activity level, quality of life, rerupture rate, revision surgery, or persistent knee-related complaints at final follow-up. However, there was a significant interaction between treatment group and time for the subjective IKDC score. Patients treated without postoperative bracing showed stable or slightly improved subjective knee function, whereas patients treated with a brace demonstrated a significant decline between one and five years. DISCUSSION: Brace-free rehabilitation after isolated ACL reconstruction with hamstring tendon autograft remains safe and effective more than five years after surgery. Postoperative bracing did not reduce rerupture rates, revision surgery, or long-term functional impairment. Instead, brace-free rehabilitation demonstrated a more favorable longitudinal development of subjective knee function. These findings further question the routine postoperative prescription of rehabilitative knee braces following isolated ACL reconstruction.

metadata.title: Efficacy of combined therapies on degenerative joint disease of the temporomandibular joint: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of intra-articular orthobiologics versus standard active control (arthrocentesis or hyaluronic acid) on pain, mouth opening and structural bone gain in advanced degenerative temporomandibular joint (TMJ) disease, stratified by orthobiologic class and joint compartment. DESIGN: Systematic review with exploratory meta-analysis, following PRISMA and prospectively registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261425634), of RCTs published January 2020-June 2026. Outcomes were pooled as mean difference (MD) by orthobiologic class, with joint compartment as a three-level moderator. Clinical relevance was assessed against minimal important difference (MCID) thresholds; non-randomised studies were synthesised narratively. RESULTS: Twenty-eight studies were included: 18 RCTs (≈862 patients; 12 pooled) and 10 narrative studies. Versus hyaluronic acid, orthobiologics reduced pain (MD -0.71) and improved mouth opening (MD 3.04 mm), both below the MCID. Versus arthrocentesis alone, effects were larger: pain (MD -1.57, exceeding the MCID) and mouth opening (MD 3.46 mm, below the MCID), with high heterogeneity unexplained by orthobiologic class. No RCT tested the dual joint space approach, represented only by one narrative study. A subset of studies had incomplete degenerative anchoring or unreported compartment. Certainty of evidence was low to very low. CONCLUSIONS: Current evidence does not support a firm recommendation for any single orthobiologic in advanced degenerative TMJ disease, reinforcing a conservative, stepwise approach. Dual joint space therapy - a plausible but untested hypothesis - remains unstudied and is a priority for future research.

metadata.title: Outcomes of open and endoscopic excision of a symptomatic os trigonum in athletes: a systematic review with exploratory analysis of prognostic factors.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: A symptomatic os trigonum causes posterior ankle impingement in athletes and is excised when conservative treatment fails. Previous syntheses have pooled mean outcomes across mixed populations, and poor outcomes have not been defined consistently. METHODS: Six databases were searched for open or endoscopic os trigonum excision in athletes, following PRISMA 2020 and SWiM. Techniques were compared within comparative studies, with supplementary pooling. A composite poor-outcome profile and eight candidate factors were examined at study-arm level. RESULTS: Thirteen studies (17 arms, 440 participants) were included. Failure to return to prior level was uncommon (9 of 438; 0-6.2% by arm). In the randomised trial, return to prior sport level was 4.4 weeks faster after endoscopic excision (95% confidence interval [CI] 2.7-6.1); pooling two further non-randomised studies with imputed SDs gave 4.9 weeks (95% CI 3.3-6.6). Trial complications occurred in 1 of 26 endoscopic and 6 of 26 open patients (odds ratio 7.50, 95% CI 0.83-67.49); the two-study pooled odds ratio was 5.59 (95% CI 1.10-28.35) from 10 events. Both nerve injuries described as permanent followed open surgery. The composite depended on arm size and threshold choice, and five of eight candidate factors could not be tested. CONCLUSION: Poor outcomes are uncommon after either approach. Low-certainty evidence suggests faster return to sport after endoscopic excision; complication evidence is of very low certainty, though no nerve injury described as permanent followed endoscopic excision. A consensus definition of return to sport is needed.

metadata.title: Cold-Water Immersion for Post-exercise Recovery: An Overlap-Aware Umbrella Review.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cold-water immersion (CWI) is widely used after strenuous exercise, but review-level findings vary by outcome, comparator, recovery window, population, and protocol. Reuse of the same primary studies across reviews can also exaggerate apparent consistency. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, Cochrane Library, Embase, and Scopus from inception to 30 January 2026 for systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and network meta-analyses of post-exercise CWI. Fourteen reviews were included. Primary-study overlap was quantified using the corrected covered area (CCA) overall and for outcome-specific study-to-review mappings. Because overlap was high and review-level estimates were statistically dependent, we did not perform second-order meta-analysis. Source-verified estimates were synthesized in a structured, overlap-aware format. Methodological quality was assessed with AMSTAR 2. RESULTS: Of the 14 included reviews, 13 provided quantitative estimates, whereas one review provided narrative evidence on heart rate variability (HRV). Overall CCA was 12.68% (high); 99 of 165 primary-study families appeared in at least two reviews. Outcome-specific CCA was 15.03% for delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS; very high) and ranged from 0.00% for interleukin-6 (IL-6) to 25.00% for C-reactive protein (CRP). It was not calculable for HRV, because one review contributed. AMSTAR 2 confidence was low in 2 reviews and critically low in 12. DOMS showed the most consistent favorable pattern: source-review standardized mean differences ranged from -1.04 to -0.37, although the largest estimate was soccer-specific and its 95% prediction interval crossed zero. Because DOMS evidence was highly redundant across the contributing reviews, this apparent consistency does not represent independent replications. Findings for objective performance and biochemical outcomes were inconsistent, time-dependent, or comparator-dependent. CONCLUSIONS: Within the available review-level evidence, CWI was associated with the most consistent reduction in self-reported short-term post-exercise DOMS, but the clinical importance of the observed effects remains uncertain. Evidence does not support a uniform benefit across objective performance or inflammatory outcomes. Protocol observations, including commonly studied temperatures and durations, are descriptive and should not be interpreted as an optimized prescription. Trial Registration PROSPERO CRD420261332482.

metadata.title: Arthroscopic Stabilization Reduces Recurrence but May Delay Return to Sport After First-Time Traumatic Anterior Shoulder Dislocation in Elite Male Athletes: A Systematic Review.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate arthroscopic stabilization versus nonoperative management for first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation in adult athletes, with a focus on recurrent instability, return-to-play rates, and time to return to play. METHODS: Five databases were searched from inception to July 2025. Studies comparing arthroscopic stabilization versus nonoperative management in adult athletes (≥18 years) with first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation were included. The primary outcome was recurrent instability. Secondary outcomes included return-to-play rates and time to return to play. A narrative synthesis was performed given the nonrandomized and heterogeneous nature of included studies. Evidence certainty was assessed using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation. RESULTS: Five studies (232 participants: 111 operative, 121 nonoperative) were included. Recurrent instability rates ranged from 3% to 14% in the operative group and 24% to 80% in the nonoperative group. Return-to-play rates were high for both approaches (operative: 93%-100%; nonoperative: 97%-100%). Nonoperative management was associated with earlier return to sport (2.3-5.7 weeks vs 18.7-39.3 weeks for operative management in studies reporting this outcome). All studies involved elite athletes, with female athletes substantially under-represented. CONCLUSIONS: Arthroscopic stabilization was consistently associated with lower rates of recurrent instability than nonoperative management after first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation but required a longer time to return to play. Nonoperative management enabled an earlier return to play but was associated with higher recurrence. The evidence is limited primarily to male military, collegiate, and professional athletes, restricting generalizability to female, recreational, and broader adult athletic populations. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, systematic review of Level II and III studies.

metadata.title: Orthobiologics for hand and wrist disorders: An indication-specific systematic review and evidence-gap synthesis.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Orthobiologics are increasingly used in hand and wrist disorders; however, their clinical effectiveness remains uncertain due to heterogeneity in indications, formulations, and outcome reporting. METHODS: This systematic review was reported in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261359867). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Web of Science were searched from inception through March 31, 2026. Primary clinical studies evaluating locally delivered orthobiologics for hand or wrist disorders were eligible. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB 2 for randomized trials and ROBINS-I for nonrandomized comparative studies and the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist for uncontrolled case series; certainty was evaluated using GRADE. Because the studies differed substantially in indication, biologic formulation, comparator, follow-up, and outcome definition, meta-analysis was not clinically appropriate; a structured qualitative synthesis was performed. RESULTS: Ten primary clinical studies were included: three studies of carpal tunnel syndrome, one of de Quervain tenosynovitis, three of trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis, one of distal-radius fracture, and two of scaphoid nonunion. No meta-analysis was performed. Evidence for carpal tunnel syndrome was inconsistent across comparators and follow-up durations. In de Quervain tenosynovitis, PRP produced outcomes comparable to corticosteroid injection, with fewer reported local adverse effects. Evidence for trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis was limited and comparator-dependent. In scaphoid nonunion, the primary BMP studies suggested possible osteoinductive benefit but also identified complications, including heterotopic ossification, persistent nonunion, and reoperation. Overall certainty ranged from moderate to very low. CONCLUSIONS: Orthobiologic effectiveness for hand and wrist disorders appears indication-specific but is supported by limited and heterogeneous evidence. Routine PRP use in osteoarthritis is not supported, and application in other conditions should remain selective and context-dependent. Larger, adequately powered, placebo-controlled trials with standardized biologic characterization and outcome reporting are required. These findings should be interpreted as an evidence-gap map rather than proof of comparative efficacy. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV (systematic review of predominantly small randomized and nonrandomized studies with heterogeneous designs and limited sample sizes).

metadata.title: Eight-week omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supplementation alters but does not attenuate exercise-induced muscle damage in older adults: a randomised controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) serves as a model to study muscle plasticity and recovery. Exercise recovery declines with age, and while omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n-3 PUFA) exhibit inconsistent effects in younger adults, the effect in older adults is unknown. METHODS: In a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial, 43 healthy, older women and men (65-85 years) ingested 5 mL of n-3 PUFA algae oil (2 g PUFA) or placebo for eight weeks. After eight weeks participants performed a bout of 10 × 10 eccentric-emphasised leg extensions. Outcome measures included quadriceps maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), muscle soreness, creatine kinase (CK) and inflammation (Interleukin-6, high-sensitive C-reactive protein; CRP) assessed at baseline and post-exercise. RESULTS: EIMD symptoms such as muscle soreness and function were modest and consistent with previous reports in older adults. Overall, n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery. However, a borderline greater MVC loss was observed in the n-3 PUFA group (time × group: P = .064), which resulted from significantly lower MVC in the n-3 PUFA group at 24 h (difference: -10.9%, 95%CI: -21.4;-0.40%, P = .042) and at 72 h (difference: -9.80, 95%CI: -18.3;-1.27, P = .025) post-exercise compared to the placebo. No significant overall group differences were observed for CK, interleukin-6, CRP, but CK concentrations significantly increased from baseline at 24 h post-exercise in the placebo group (change: +81.1%, 95%CI:10.5;152%, P = .014). Habitual physical activity and sex emerged as significant moderators of molecular recovery in an exploratory analysis. CONCLUSION: n-3 PUFA supplementation did not improve functional recovery, but different molecular response patterns were observed. Habitual physical activity and sex may be determinants of post-exercise response; this exploratory finding warrants confirmation in larger studies.

metadata.title: Anthocyanin-Rich Aronia melanocarpa Supplementation Modulates Intestinal Barrier Biomarkers and Stress-Axis Response in a Randomized Controlled Trial.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Anthocyanin-rich berries may modulate intestinal barrier-related processes and physiological stress responses, but evidence from human studies remains limited. METHODS: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial included 15 elite male rowers (Aronia group, n = 7; placebo group, n = 8). Participants received Aronia melanocarpa supplementation or placebo for eight weeks and performed a standardized 2000-m rowing ergometer test before and after the intervention. Circulating claudin-3 (CLDN-3), lipopolysaccharide-binding protein (LBP), intestinal fatty acid-binding protein (I-FABP), and cortisol concentrations were assessed before exercise, immediately after exercise, and following 1 h of recovery. RESULTS: A significant Group × Time interaction was observed for CLDN-3 (p = 0.0463). After eight weeks, pre-exercise CLDN-3 concentrations were lower in the Aronia group than in the placebo group (p = 0.0367). Lower pre-exercise LBP concentrations (p = 0.0125) and lower cortisol concentrations at 1 h post-exercise (p = 0.0079) were also observed in the Aronia group compared with placebo. No significant supplementation-specific effect was observed for I-FABP. CONCLUSIONS: Eight weeks of Aronia melanocarpa supplementation was associated with differences in selected intestinal barrier-related biomarkers and post-exercise cortisol concentrations in elite male rowers. However, these findings were primarily related to specific sampling time points and should not be interpreted as evidence of improved intestinal barrier function. Given the small sample size and potential dietary confounding, the results are preliminary and require confirmation in larger randomized controlled trials.

metadata.title: Paraspinal Muscle Quality and Functional Outcomes Following Lumbar Fusion: A Systematic Review.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: Lumbar interbody fusion (LIF) procedures are associated with postoperative paraspinal muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration (FI), which may influence long-term pain and functional recovery. However, the relationship between muscle quality, both pre- and postoperatively, and patient-reported outcomes remains unclear for patients undergoing lumbar fusion. This correlation was compared between minimally invasive surgery (MIS) and conventional open surgery (COS) approaches to assess differences in postoperative muscle preservation and functional outcomes. METHODS: A systematic review, conducted following PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420250650064), examined studies found in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science through February 2025. Studies were included if they assessed adult patients undergoing LIF with preoperative CT or MRI evaluation of the multifidus (MF) or erector spinae (ES) and reported postoperative cross-sectional area (CSA), FI, or patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs). RESULTS: Twenty studies met inclusion criteria; risk of bias was assessed with ROBINS-I for 19 non-randomized studies and RoB 2 for one randomized trial. Seven of nine COS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, including all three COS-only studies, measured by CSA and FI. Two of twelve MIS intervention studies found significant pre- to postoperative muscle damage, with four of six direct comparisons found smaller declines in CSA, increases in FI, or both after MIS compared to COS in at least one muscle or setting. Higher preoperative muscle quality, particularly lower FI, and smaller pre- to postoperative muscle changes were associated with greater PROM improvements. Across the PROM-focused studies, four of the five reported that higher preoperative CSA or lower FI predicted better postoperative improvements in functional outcomes, with one identifying that MF FI of 61% or greater as a threshold for failing to achieve clinically meaningful ODI improvements. CONCLUSION: MIS techniques were associated with a decrease in pre- to postoperative FI compared with COS, although PROM improvement occurred across both approaches. While preoperative paraspinal muscle quality and size decreases are generally smaller with better functional outcomes following postoperative LIF, this relationship is not consistently observed across all studies or surgical techniques. These findings suggest that the current imaging-based biomarkers may not fully capture the multifactorial nature of functional recovery and underscore the need for further research into additional predictors of muscle recovery.

metadata.title: Stress Fracture Recovery and Return to Sports in Youth with Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare stress fracture recovery times in children with and without juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), and to evaluate JIA-related factors associated with recovery. STUDY DESIGN: This retrospective case-control study included children with JIA <19 years old with a first stress fracture treated at a single center from 2004-2024. Cases were matched 1:3 to children without JIA by age, gender, and fracture location. Recovery time was defined from imaging confirmation of a stress fracture to medical clearance to return to sports. We used a generalized estimating equations method to compare recovery times and evaluate associations with JIA-related factors, including JIA subtype, glucocorticoid and arthritis-directed therapy exposure, and proximity of arthritis to fracture location. RESULTS: The cohort included 260 children (65 cases, 195 controls; 53.8% female; median age 14.3 years [IQR 12.6, 16.2]). Pars interarticularis fractures accounted for 30.8% of injuries, followed by metatarsal (23.1%), and tibial fractures (14.2%). Among children with JIA who sustained pars fractures, 75.0% had an enthesitis-related arthritis (ERA) phenotype. Median recovery times were 10.6 (IQR 7.0, 19.4) weeks for children with JIA and 10.6 (IQR 7.1, 14.6) weeks for controls (P=0.197), with no significant differences for lower-extremity fractures. In contrast, children with JIA who sustained pars fractures had longer recovery times than controls (ratio of geometric means: 1.44, 95% CI 1.01, 2.05; P=0.045). Among children with active sacroiliitis, fractures occurred more frequently in the proximate pars or pelvis than at non-proximate sites (P<0.001). Recovery time was not associated with JIA subtype (all p>0.150), glucocorticoid exposure (P=0.365), or biologic therapy (P=0.625). CONCLUSIONS: Overall recovery times did not differ significantly between children with and without JIA. However, children with JIA and pars fractures had longer recovery times, and associations with ERA and sacroiliitis warrant further investigation. Additional research on spondylolysis recovery in young athletes with JIA may help inform individualized return-to-sports recommendations.

metadata.title: Sex-Equitable Machine Learning Prediction of Ankle Reinjury in Individuals with Chronic Ankle Instability: A 2-Year Prospective Cohort Study with Fairness Audit.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Patients with chronic ankle instability (CAI) face a 2-year reinjury rate approaching 50%, but individualized prediction models that quantify which baseline impairments predict subsequent reinjury within an established CAI cohort remain scarce, and existing prediction models for ankle injury have not assessed sex-related fairness. The aim was to develop and internally validate sex-equitable machine learning (ML) models predicting 2-year ankle reinjury in individuals with CAI, identify the most influential baseline prognostic markers, and audit sex-stratified model performance. METHODS: One hundred physically active individuals (50 male, 50 female) with CAI (mean age 21.8 ± 2.3 years) were recruited from a university population between February 2017 and February 2018 and prospectively followed for 2 years; 96 (49 male, 47 female) with at least one follow-up response were retained for analysis (41 reinjury events, 43% reinjury rate). Fourteen baseline predictors spanning demographic, anthropometric, injury-history, patient-reported, biomechanical, postural-control, and functional-performance domains were collected. Six algorithms were trained with nested cross-validation: an unpenalized logistic regression baseline and five ML algorithms (Elastic Net, support vector machine, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM). Predictive contribution of each feature was quantified using Shapley additive explanations and partial-dependence plots. A pre-specified fairness audit compared single global and sex-specific Youden thresholds derived out-of-fold using the equalized-odds gap and disproportionate-impact ratio. RESULTS: All algorithms achieved area under the curve (AUC) values above 0.70; Elastic Net was selected as the primary model (AUC = 0.807, 95% CI 0.714-0.893; calibration slope = 1.015). Sex, arch height index, previous sprains, dorsiflexion range of motion, and Biodex Overall Stability Index consistently emerged as the most influential prognostic markers. Within-sex discrimination was comparable between males and females, but a single global threshold produced an equalized-odds gap of 0.384 that was reduced by 57% (to 0.164) through sex-specific thresholding without retraining the model. CONCLUSIONS: ML models with a fairness-audited threshold strategy predicted 2-year ankle reinjury in individuals with CAI, reducing the equalized-odds gap by 57%, though the disproportionate-impact ratio (0.683) remained below the 0.80 benchmark. External validation is required before clinical deployment.

metadata.title: Influence of ballistic and conventional resistance training on bone properties in postmenopausal women: A randomised controlled trial.
metadata.abstract: High-load conventional resistance training (CRT) is recommended for osteoporosis prevention. Ballistic resistance training (BRT) involves high velocity and impact forces with lower loads. The Resistance Exercise Programme on Risk of Osteoporosis and Osteoarthritis in Females (REPROOF) study examined effects of BRT and CRT, relative to control (CON) on proximal femur BMD. Healthy postmenopausal women aged 50-70 years were randomised into BRT, CRT or CON groups. BRT and CRT conducted supervised resistance training twice weekly for eight months. In CRT, concentric and eccentric phases each lasted ~2 s at 55-80% of one-repetition maximum (1RM). BRT involved explosive (maximum velocity) concentric movements at 20-50% of 1RM. Proximal femur and lumbar spine BMD were measured by DXA; tibia structure by peripheral QCT. Groups were compared using ANCOVA, adjusting for baseline values. Of 109 women randomised, 82 (63.1 ± 3.7 years; 24.5 ± 3.5 kgm-2; femoral neck T-score -1.1 ± 0.8) completed the study, with 98% adherence. BRT improved total hip BMD (+0.008 [0.001, 0.014] g/cm2; P = 0.02) versus CON. CRT did not affect hip BMD but tibial shaft cortical BMD increased (+4.141 [1.007, 7.274] g/cm2; P = 0.01) and cortical thickness declined relative to CON (-0.07 [-0.13, -0.01] mm; P = 0.03), accompanied by tibial shaft widening. BRT increased total hip and trochanter BMD (P ≤ 0.03) in the subgroup with low BMD. BRT benefitted proximal femur BMD relative to CON, including in the subgroup with low BMD. CRT did not affect hip BMD but caused tibial shaft structural adaptation that may affect strength in bending. BRT based interventions should be further developed and evaluated for osteoporosis prevention.

metadata.title: Characterising the Internal and External Load During Warm-Up, Match Play and Training in Soccer Substitutes: A Systematic Scoping Review.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Shorter match-play exposure for soccer substitutes relative to those who start matches has implications in the days before, during and following match play concerning their training, preparatory and recovery/compensatory practices. Specifically, characterising the internal and external loading of substitute players throughout a weekly microcycle can facilitate evidence-based recommendations aimed at optimising their performance readiness. OBJECTIVES: This systematic scoping review aimed to map and characterise the internal and external loading associated with warm-up, match play and training in soccer substitutes. METHODS: Prior to literature searches being conducted, a Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Study design (PICOS) statement was formed. Online database (PubMed, SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Web of Science) searches were performed according to PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) protocols. Studies were eligible if internal or external characteristics of soccer substitutes were measured in training or match-play scenarios. After calibration exercises, two authors independently quality assessed each study, with Cohen's kappa undertaken to assess inter-rater agreement. A scoping review methodology was selected because of the methodological and conceptual heterogeneity across studies, which precluded meaningful meta-analysis. RESULTS: A total of 5135 studies were identified, 66 of which met study criteria. Substantive inter-rater agreement was observed (κ = 0.939, p < 0.001) during the quality assessment of included studies. Soccer substitutes' body temperature, and thus several aspects of physical performance, may not be maintained at time of pitch entry (body temperature pre-pitch entry ~ 37 °C vs match play > 38 °C). Substitutes may experience lower absolute physical loading during training and match day (e.g. match-day 'top up' activity: ~ 17 min; total distance: ~ 1700 m) but during match play, substitutes typically cover higher relative total distances (~ 109 to ~ 137 m·min-1), high-speed running (~ 9.8 to ~ 13.5 m·min-1) and sprinting distance (~ 3.8 to 5.0 m·min-1) compared with players who started the match. Substitutes playing in the second-half exhibit increased heart rates compared with full-match players (84% vs 81% maximum heart rate); however, this remains lower than the first-half heart rate responses of full-match players (84% vs 86% maximum heart rate). CONCLUSIONS: This systematic scoping review summarises current evidence and key findings relating to the internal and external characteristics of soccer substitutes during warm-up, match play and training that can be used in practice to inform player welfare and sport science support within these cohorts. Chiefly, during match-day warm-ups, soccer substitutes' body temperature and physical performance responses may not be maintained, despite typical substitute-specific match-day practices being employed. Similarly, soccer substitutes were frequently reported to demonstrate higher relative total distance, high-speed running and sprinting outputs compared with starting players. Further research is needed to better understand performance demands, longitudinal adaptations, contextual influences and female-specific responses in soccer substitutes.
