metadata.title: Low energy availability in recreational high-intensity functional training athletes: associations with health and performance outcomes.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Low energy availability (LEA) is the primary etiological factor underlying Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S), yet limited research has examined LEA risk and associated health and performance outcomes in recreational high-intensity functional training (HIFT) athletes. The purpose of this study was to evaluate energy availability (EA) and physiological outcomes aligned with the RED-S Health and Performance Models in a recreational HIFT cohort. METHODS: Thirty participants (females: n = 18, males: n = 12; 31.2 ± 8.2 years) completed a two-week prospective observational study with repeated measures of energy intake, exercise energy expenditure, and associated health and performance-related measures. Energy intake was assessed via dietary logs, exercise energy expenditure was estimated using a wearable armband, and EA was calculated relative to dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry-derived fat-free mass. Participants were classified as LEA if EA was <30 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1. Performance-related outcomes included rating of perceived exertion (RPE), perceived recovery status (PRS), and total quality recovery (TQR). Health-related outcomes included sleep duration, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and bone mineral density (BMD) (reported by Z-Score). RESULTS: Mean EA was 24.9 ± 9.7 kcal·kg-1 FFM·day-1, with 80% (n = 24) of participants demonstrating EA below the LEA classification threshold. The high prevalence of LEA should be interpreted cautiously given the potential for underreporting dietary intake. LEA status was not associated with differences in recovery, sleep quality, or BMD (p > 0.05), and EA was not significantly correlated with performance or health outcomes. In an exploratory analysis, sleep duration was moderately positively associated with TQR (ρ = 0.46, p = 0.01); however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously given the number of comparisons performed. DISCUSSION: Despite the high prevalence of LEA, associated health and performance impairments were not detected, suggesting that measurable consequences of LEA may not be evident over a short observation period in recreational HIFT athletes. These findings support ongoing monitoring of EA, fueling practices, and recovery behaviors to reduce the potential long-term consequences associated with RED-S.

metadata.title: Conceptual Frameworks and Assessment of Readiness to Train in Endurance Exercise: A Systematic Review.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: Readiness to train has emerged as a construct to guide daily training prescription and recovery management in endurance athletes. However, its conceptual basis, assessment, and methodological quality and validity remain inconsistently defined. This systematic review aimed to (1) identify how readiness is defined in endurance exercise and (2) categorize tools used to assess it. As a secondary aim, the review evaluated the methodological approach of the studies employing these tools. METHODS: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were explored. Eligible studies included endurance athletes aged 18-65 years, evaluating readiness before or after training or competition. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed quality using the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. Fourteen studies were included. RESULTS: Readiness definitions were inconsistent and frequently overlapped with related constructs such as recovery and fatigue. Ten studies used self-reported tools (fatigue, sleep, stress, and soreness). Nine studies assessed objective tools, including heart rate (HR) variability, resting HR, countermovement jump, and submaximal tests. HR variability-based approaches and individualized feedback were used to track autonomic recovery and guide training prescription, while on-field indices (eg, HR-running speed, HR-running power, countermovement jump) provided neuromuscular insights, although they can also be influenced by cardiovascular and metabolic factors. Overall, there was considerable heterogeneity in tools and their combinations, highlighting the lack of standardized approaches to assess readiness to train. Seven studies combined subjective and objective measures, suggesting a more comprehensive monitoring strategy. However, many of these tools were primarily used to assess related constructs (eg, fatigue, recovery, and training adaptation) rather than directly predict performance; consequently, their ability to predict performance outcomes remained limited or was not even assessed. CONCLUSION: This review highlights substantial conceptual ambiguity, methodological limitations, and heterogeneity in readiness assessment. A multidimensional framework conceptualizing readiness as a dynamic psychophysiological state influenced by stress, recovery, and contextual factors may support more structured and meaningful monitoring in endurance athletes.

metadata.title: Diagnosis, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport after Athletic Hamstring Injury: An ICCUS Society Consensus Statement.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Athletic hamstring injuries (AHSI) remain a persistent challenge because recurrence is common and clinical decisions often depend on incomplete evidence. This consensus statement is intended to give clinicians a practical, unified framework for classification, rehabilitation, and return to sport after athletic hamstring injury. The purpose of this study was to achieve expert consensus on the management of athletic hamstring injuries through a structured, scientific survey approach. STUDY DESIGN: Delphi Survey. METHODS: A modified Delphi process, aligned with CREDES guidelines, was conducted with an expert panel of sports physical therapists identified as having specific expertise in AHSI from the ICCUS Society. Consensus was defined a priori as at least 80% agreement or disagreement on a 5-point Likert scale. Statements addressed three areas: AHSI examination and classification, rehabilitation and management, and return to sport (RTS) testing. RESULTS: Sixty statements were developed across three domains. Seventeen experienced clinicians completed the final round. Overall, 54 statements reached consensus, with a mean Likert score of 4.56 ± 0.37 out of 5 (strongly agree), and mean agreement of 89.88% ± 12.1%. Experts supported standardized terminology, MRI and the use of diagnostic ultrasound for diagnosis when appropriate, individualized and criterion-based rehabilitation, progressive tissue loading and length restoration, early neuromuscular control, gradual running and agility progression, progression to pain-free sprinting, objective strength assessment, sport-specific workloads, and athlete readiness as key RTS criteria. DISCUSSION: The findings emphasize active rehabilitation guided by measurable progress rather than reliance on fixed thresholds. Clinicians should combine injury classification, functional presentation, symptom response, objective testing, sport demands, and athlete confidence when advancing rehabilitation and making RTS decisions. CONCLUSION: This ICCUS Society consensus statement offers a practical roadmap for managing AHSI: classify clearly, load progressively, monitor symptoms, test objectively, and return athletes only when sport-specific running, sprinting, strength, training tolerance, and readiness align. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: 4.

metadata.title: Association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden in NCAA Division I athletes.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To examine the association between sleep difficulty and baseline concussion-like symptom burden among NCAA Division I athletes and whether sleep difficulty is associated with neurocognitive performance. METHODS: This cross-sectional analysis included 584 NCAA Division I student-athletes. Sleep difficulty was assessed using the Athlete Sleep Screening Questionnaire Sleep Difficulty Score (SDS), and symptom burden using the 24-item SCOAT6 Symptom Evaluation. Symptom number was analyzed with multivariable negative binomial regression and symptom severity with multivariable linear regression using HC3 robust standard errors. Models adjusted for age, sex, sport type, and head-injury history. Sensitivity analyses excluded overlapping sleep-related symptoms and examined individual symptoms, symptom domains, head-injury strata, and neurocognitive outcomes. RESULTS: Each 1-point increase in SDS was associated with greater symptom number (n = 583; IRR = 1.127, 95% CI 1.086-1.169, P < .001) and severity (n = 584; B = 1.054, 95% CI 0.688-1.419, P < .001). Associations persisted after excluding sleep disturbance and after additionally excluding fatigue/low energy and drowsiness. Twenty-one of 24 symptoms remained associated with SDS after false-discovery-rate correction. Head-injury history did not modify associations with symptom number (P = .971) or severity (P = .846). SDS was not associated with memory (B = -0.012, P = .269), executive function (B = -0.017, P = .247), or psychomotor speed (B = 0.001, P = .939). CONCLUSIONS: Greater self-reported sleep difficulty was associated with greater baseline concussion-like symptom burden but not with assessed neurocognitive outcomes. Sleep difficulty should be considered a contextual factor when interpreting baseline concussion symptom reports.

metadata.title: Anterior cruciate ligament injuries in women's professional football: Higher incidence and distinct injury patterns compared to men.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries are more frequent in female football players, but sex-specific differences in injury characteristics remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to analyse sex-specific differences in ACL injury incidence and characteristics in professional football. METHODS: This prospective cohort study used data from a German national ACL registry ('Kreuzbandregister im Deutschen Fußball'), including professional male (first to third league) and female (first and second league) football players from the 2016/2017 to 2024/2025 seasons. Incidence rates were compared using Poisson regression (incidence rate ratio, IRR) and injury characteristics using multivariable logistic regression. RESULTS: A total of 459 ACL injuries were analysed (177 female and 282 male). The rate was 1.19 versus 0.69 per 1000 match hours (IRR 1.69, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.34-2.13). The difference was most pronounced in the first division (IRR 2.49, 1.82-3.41) and smaller and not significant in the lower leagues (IRR 1.24, 0.93-1.65). Injuries in female players were more often non-contact (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.37) and indirect-contact injuries (aOR 2.92), occurred more often on artificial turf (aOR 5.42) and in national team players (aOR 3.03). Concomitant injury patterns did not differ significantly, except for fewer lateral collateral ligament injuries in women. CONCLUSION: ACL injury rates are higher in female professional football players, particularly in the first division. The predominance of non-contact and indirect-contact mechanisms supports targeted, sex-specific prevention strategies. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II, prospective cohort study.

metadata.title: Risk, Knowledge, and Awareness of Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S) in Elite Female Volleyball Players.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a condition caused by low energy availability (LEA) and is associated with adverse health and performance outcomes in athletes. Although volleyball involves considerable physical stress and repetitive jumping, little is known about RED-S knowledge and risk of LEA in elite female volleyball players. HYPOTHESIS: Elite female volleyball athletes have limited awareness of RED-S, and athletes at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q are more likely to be injured. STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional study. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level 3. METHODS: Elite female volleyball athletes competing in the Turkish Women's Elite Volleyball League during the 2024-2025 season were recruited. Participants completed an online survey including demographic information, the Low Energy Availability in Females Questionnaire (LEAF-Q), and items assessing knowledge, awareness, and support-seeking behaviors related to RED-S. Athletes were classified as "at risk" for LEA using a LEAF-Q cutoff score of ≥8. Associations between LEAF-Q risk status and injury history during the previous year were analyzed. RESULTS: A total of 148 athletes participated. The mean LEAF-Q score was 5.50 ± 3.48, and 25% of athletes were classified as at risk for LEA according to the LEAF-Q. Most athletes (92.6%) reported never having heard of RED-S or the Female Athlete Triad. Athletes identified as at risk by the LEAF-Q were significantly more likely to have sustained an injury in the previous year than athletes not at risk (odds ratio, 7.86; 95% CI, 3.03-20.41). CONCLUSION: Elite female volleyball athletes demonstrated low knowledge of RED-S, while a substantial proportion were identified as at risk for LEA. LEA risk was associated strongly with injury history, supporting the clinical relevance of LEAF-Q screening in this population. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine LEAF-Q screening combined with sport-specific education may facilitate early identification of athletes who may require further clinical evaluation for LEA-related problems and may inform prevention-oriented support strategies in elite female volleyball players.

metadata.title: Long-term market value decline after medial collateral ligament injury in professional football players did not differ statistically significantly from matched non-injured controls: A Transfermarkt-based cohort study.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: The aim of this study was to characterize the longitudinal trajectory of estimated market value after medial collateral ligament (MCL) injury in professional football players and determine whether postinjury changes differed from matched non-injured controls. METHODS: Professional football players with a recorded MCL injury were identified from Transfermarkt injury records labeled as medial (collateral) ligament injuries (seasons 2007/08-2023/24); duplicate records of the same episode were merged, and injuries were not clinically verified. Market value was assessed during the season preceding injury (Tpre), the injury season (T0), and annually for five subsequent seasons (T1-T5). Linear mixed-effect models evaluated longitudinal changes and associations with age, playing position, league level, and injury-related absence. Segmented models assessed changes in temporal trajectory. MCL cases were also matched 1:2 to non-injured controls by competition, season, playing position, age, and preinjury market value, with group differences examined using a difference-in-differences model. RESULTS: Forty-five players with 50 MCL injury episodes were included, 8 of which had an associated anterior cruciate ligament or meniscal lesion. Median age at injury was 26.5 years (interquartile range [IQR]: 23.0-28.7), and median time lost was 42 days (IQR: 21-76.5). In the adjusted model, market value did not differ statistically significantly from Tpre at T0 (P = 0.649), T1 (P = 0.813), or T2 (P = 0.064) but was statistically significantly lower at T3 (-34.25%; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -51.21% to -11.38%; P = 0.006), T4 (-47.54%; 95% CI: -61.54% to -28.43%; P < 0.001), and T5 (-51.70%; 95% CI: -65.25% to -32.88%; P < 0.001). No statistically significant postinjury change in slope was observed (P = 0.103). Thirty-one of 48 eligible cases were matched to 62 controls; the remaining 17 had no eligible control within the matching criteria, mostly because of lower-tier competition or low preinjury market value. Difference-in-differences estimates were not statistically significant at any time point (P = 0.167-0.561; range: -10.9% [95% CI: -39.2% to 30.6%] at T0 to -24.6% [95% CI: -49.5% to 12.6%] at T3); the study could detect only differences of approximately 42%-46% or more. Results were unchanged when analyses were restricted to isolated MCL injuries. CONCLUSIONS: Market value declined substantially during long-term follow-up after MCL injury, but this decline was not statistically significantly different from that observed in matched non-injured players (P = 0.167-0.561). Much of the apparent long-term depreciation may therefore reflect the underlying age- and career-related trajectory of professional footballers; however, the matched analysis was underpowered, and a modest injury-specific effect, particularly after more severe injuries with longer absence, cannot be excluded. Because injury grade and treatment were unavailable, these findings should not be generalized to high-grade or operatively treated MCL injuries. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III, retrospective comparative cohort study.

metadata.title: Return to Sport and Clinical Outcomes after Surgical Stabilization of Chronic Ankle Instability in Athletes.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic ankle instability (CAI) can compromise athletic performance and delay return to competition. Although primary ligament repair and ligament reconstruction are valid surgical options, comparative data remains limited. PURPOSE: The primary aim was to evaluate overall return-to-sport outcomes after surgical stabilization of chronic ankle instability in athletes. The secondary aim was to compare return-to-sport and postoperative clinical outcomes between direct ligament repair and ligament reconstruction. STUDY DESIGN: Comparative retrospective study METHODS: This comparative cohort study included 54 athletes who underwent surgical stabilization for CAI between 2018 and 2024. Surgical procedures were categorized as primary repair and ligament reconstruction. The primary outcomes were RTS status and time to RTS. Secondary outcomes included postoperative Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM) scores and residual complaints. RESULTS: The mean age was 25.6 ± 6.9 years, and 48% of patients were football players. The median interval from the latest injury to surgery was 6.0 months. RTS status was available for 49 of the 54 athletes (91%). Of these, 48 (98%) returned to sport at a mean time of 5.3 months (range 2.0 to 16.0), while one athlete did not return to sport. Postoperative functional outcomes were favorable, with mean FAAM activities of daily living and sport scores of 96.2 ± 8.3 and 89.7 ± 20.4, respectively. No statistically significant differences were observed among surgical groups in RTS status, time to RTS, FAAM scores, or residual complaints. CONCLUSION: Surgical stabilization of chronic ankle instability was associated with favorable postoperative scores and a high RTS rate among athletes with available outcome data. The sample size and overall study design preclude conclusions regarding the equivalence or superiority of repair versus reconstruction.

metadata.title: Hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement in American football athletes: examining factors associated with outcomes at a mean follow-up time of 6.3 years.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Femoroacetabular impingement (FAIS) is a common cause of hip pain and performance limitation in athletes. Hip arthroscopy is the gold standard of treatment in professional American football athletes, with numerous studies demonstrating favorable outcomes and high return-to-sport (RTS) rates. However, limited outcomes data exists in collegiate athletes and fewer still in high school athletes. The purpose of this study was to evaluate long-term patient-reported outcomes (PROs), RTS rates, and predictors of outcomes following hip arthroscopy for symptomatic FAIS in high school and collegiate football athletes. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was performed which included high-school and collegiate football athletes who underwent hip arthroscopy for symptomatic FAIS. Outcomes were assessed using the modified Harris Hip Score (mHHS), International Hip Outcome Tool-12 (IHOT-12), and Hip Outcomes Score-Sport Specific Subscale (HOS-Sport). Data regarding return to preinjury sport were also collected. Pre-operative radiographic data, including alpha angle, lateral center edge angle, and Tönnis grade, were collected. RESULTS: This cohort had a mean post-operative follow up of 6.3 years, with mean PRO scores of 82.2 on the mHHS, 84.6 on the iHOT-12, and 88.3 on the HOS-Sport. PASS thresholds were achieved by 69%, 77% and 80% of athletes for the same outcomes, respectively. 60% of the cohort attempted to return to sport, and 91% of the athletes who attempted to return to preinjury level of sport were successful. Increased age at time of surgery and larger pre-operative alpha angles were associated with worse PRO scores at follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: Hip arthroscopy for FAIS in high school and collegiate football players yielded favorable long-term outcomes and RTS rates. This is similar to current outcomes data in professional athletes. Increased alpha angle and age at surgery were associated with worse outcomes, emphasizing the importance of early recognition and appropriate surgical treatment. Comparisons of outcomes between blocking and nonblocking positions may warrant further investigation in larger cohorts.

metadata.title: Most National Football League Players Return to Play After Achilles Tendon Repair, Yet Only One-Half Regain Preinjury Performance With Persistent Pass-Rush Decline at Year 2.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate National Football League (NFL) player performance using advanced statistics after Achilles tendon (AT) repair. METHODS: NFL players who underwent AT repair between 2017 and 2023 were identified from a publicly available injury database. Demographic and performance data were collected preinjury and up to 2 seasons postinjury, with a minimum follow-up of 1 regular-season game required to assess return to play (RTP). RTP was defined as being active for a regular-season game and return to performance as achieving ≥90% of preinjury performance. Performance was assessed using Sports Information Solutions' points above replacement (PAR). Factors associated with RTP and return to performance were analyzed using binary logistic regression, with pre- and postinjury performance compared using paired t tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, as appropriate. RESULTS: Seventy-seven NFL players with AT repairs were identified. Ten were excluded for no prior regular-season play, leaving 67 included. Overall, 77.6% (n = 52) returned to play. Increasing age reduced the odds of RTP (odds ratio 0.75, 95% confidence interval [0.60-0.95], P = .02). Index games preinjury increased the odds of RTP (odds ratio 1.12, 95% confidence interval [1.01-1.24], P = .04). Body mass index, position, index games played, and index PAR were not significant. Among returnees, 50% (n = 26) achieved at least 90% of preinjury performance. Higher index PAR predicted lower odds of meeting this threshold (odds ratio 0.77, 95% confidence interval [0.66-0.90], P = .00). Pass-rush PAR declined at year 2 after injury from 1.17 (±5.19) preinjury to -0.66 (±2.15), P = .02. CONCLUSIONS: In this study using publicly available data, 77.6% of NFL players returned to play after AT repair; however, only one-half of these players regained ≥90% of their preinjury performance. Older age reduced the likelihood of RTP, whereas more preinjury games started increased it. Higher preinjury PAR reduced the likelihood of performance recovery. Pass-rush performance declined by the second postinjury season. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV, retrospective therapeutic case series.

metadata.title: Developmental Differences in Muscle, Tendon, and Cartilage Injuries among Elite Badminton Players.
metadata.abstract: This study investigated differences in the characteristics of severe muscle, tendon, and cartilage injuries according to injury timing and post-injury management among elite badminton players. A retrospective interview study was conducted involving 126 badminton players aged 19 to 24 years. A total of 87 severe injury cases reported by 73 athletes were analyzed, with some athletes contributing more than one case. Injuries were classified according to timing into the secondary school group (n=33) and the post-secondary group (n=54). Injury characteristics and post-injury management were compared using chi-square and Fisher's exact tests, with effect sizes. Odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals examined associations with injury timing. Compared with the secondary school group, the post-secondary group had higher odds of lower limb muscle injuries (odds ratio=6.00, 95% confidence interval=1.85-19.47, p=0.003) and smash/stroke-related injuries (odds ratio=5.43, 95% confidence interval=1.15-25.66, p=0.033), whereas the post-secondary group had lower odds of lower limb tendinopathies (odds ratio=0.21, 95% confidence interval=0.08-0.55, p=0.001). These findings suggest that severe injury characteristics may differ according to the timing of injury occurrence, despite no significant between-group differences in post-injury management, and may help inform potential injury prevention priorities based on the observed injury patterns.

metadata.title: Platelet-related extracellular vesicles: Therapeutic roles in musculoskeletal disorders.
metadata.abstract: Musculoskeletal disorders are a major cause of pain, disability, and loss of function. Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated for musculoskeletal repair, and interest has increasingly extended to extracellular vesicle (EV) preparations obtained from platelet-related starting materials. These include EV-enriched preparations collected from isolated platelets or defined platelet concentrates (P-EVs), from PRP (PRP-EVs), and from platelet lysate (PL-EVs). They do not represent the same biological product. Their cellular contributors, co-isolated soluble components, and molecular composition can differ substantially, and the name of the starting material does not prove the origin of every vesicle in the preparation. Preclinical studies nevertheless suggest that these EV preparations can influence inflammatory responses, cartilage metabolism, tendon-cell behavior, and the local repair environment. The strength of this evidence varies with the source material, separation and characterization methods, experimental model, and delivery strategy. This review examines the therapeutic evidence for platelet-related EV preparations in musculoskeletal disorders, while keeping P-EVs, PRP-EVs, PL-EVs, and plasma-derived EVs distinct and considering the methodological limitations that currently restrict comparison and clinical translation.

metadata.title: Rehabilitation strategies for carpal instability: A scoping review of conservative and postsurgical interventions.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Carpal instability can cause pain, weakness, mechanical symptoms, and long-term disability. Rehabilitation is central to both conservative care and post-surgical recovery, yet clinicians face fragmented evidence. PURPOSE: To map and synthesize rehabilitation strategies for carpal instability across conservative and postsurgical pathways, and to identify gaps that limit evidence-informed practice. STUDY DESIGN: Scoping review. METHODS: JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines were followed. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, with no date restrictions, up to March 16, 2026. Findings were summarized numerically and thematically and interpreted using an ICF-oriented taxonomy. RESULTS: Fifty-nine reports published between 1990 and 2025 were included. The literature was methodologically heterogeneous, largely composed of descriptive or secondary designs. Reports addressed conservative rehabilitation, post-surgical rehabilitation, or both, with dissociative (CID) and non-dissociative (CIND) carpal instability being the most frequently addressed patterns. Rehabilitation strategies identified across the included literature were categorized into six categories: immobilization; pain/edema/scar, and education-related management; mobilization; therapeutic exercise; proprioceptive training; and instrumental/physical modalities. Immobilization and therapeutic exercise were the most frequently described components. Rehabilitation strategies varied by instability type, particularly in orthotic selection and muscle recruitment. Pain, function, strength, and range of motion were the most frequently reported outcomes, while participation-level outcomes such as return to work or sport were inconsistently addressed. Dosage, treatment progression criteria, and follow-up were variably reported across studies. CONCLUSIONS: This review provides a practical synthesis of recurring rehabilitation components across conservative and post-surgical care that may support rehabilitation planning. It also identifies key reporting gaps in intervention content, dosage, progression criteria, outcomes, and follow-up. The findings encourage a broader interpretation of carpal instability as a condition shaped not only by structural injury, but also by the interaction between passive stabilizing structures, active muscular support, motor control, and the capacity to sustain function under load and during activity.

metadata.title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: To investigate the effects of caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 and 6 mg/kg on reactive blocking timing, block-jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses in elite female volleyball players under post-fatigue conditions. METHODS: Fifteen elite female volleyball players completed a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study implemented with double-blinding procedures. Participants consumed placebo (PLA), caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 mg/kg (CAF3) or 6 mg/kg (CAF6), and were tested after supplementation and warm-up at PRE and immediately after a volleyball-specific repeated blocking fatigue protocol (POST). Primary outcomes were reactive blocking timing-chain indices and block-jump (BJ) peak power. Secondary outcomes included additional BJ mechanical variables and general jump measures from countermovement jump (CMJ) and drop jump (DJ) tests. Exploratory outcomes included synchronized surface electromyography (sEMG) variables of lower-limb muscles. Participant blinding was assessed after each visit. RESULTS: Fatigue impaired jump-related performance across conditions (p < 0.05). For the primary outcomes, the descriptive decline in BJ peak power was 6.9% in CAF6 versus 13.9% in PLA; the adjusted POST comparison did not establish superiority of CAF6 over CAF3. For timing outcomes, overall sequence time increased by 18.4% in PLA, 6.4% in CAF3, and 3.0% in CAF6; CAF6 therefore showed the smallest descriptive deterioration in the integrated sequence measure, whereas CAF3 showed little change in the mean stationary and movement component times. CAF6 showed a reduction in mean stationary response time and the smallest increase in overall sequence time. For secondary outcomes, caffeine showed more favorable post-fatigue responses in selected CMJ/DJ measures, including CMJ mean propulsive power and DJ contact time (p < 0.05), and CAF6 showed greater preservation of selected stretch-shortening cycle-related mechanical measures, including DJ jump height and DJ vertical stiffness, than PLA (p < 0.05). In contrast, CMJ mRSI showed a divergent pattern and was not interpreted as evidence of caffeine-related attenuation of fatigue-induced decrements. Exploratory sEMG results showed smaller post-fatigue changes in selected frequency-domain and activation-timing variables under CAF6, particularly in measures related to extensor-muscle function. Participant masking was incomplete: perceived caffeine ingestion was reported in 0.0%, 53.3%, and 80.0% of PLA, CAF3, and CAF6 visits, respectively, and adverse effects were more frequent in CAF6. CONCLUSIONS: The observed responses were outcome-specific: CAF6 showed a smaller decline in BJ peak power and the smallest increase in overall sequence time, whereas CAF3 showed little change in mean stationary and movement response times. These findings do not establish a generally preferable dose or a timing-stability advantage for CAF3. Incomplete participant masking limits attribution of the differences exclusively to caffeine dose.

metadata.title: Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (aronia melanocarpa) supplementation modulates exercise-induced changes in iron metabolism in female swimmers.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intense exercise may transiently alter iron metabolism through inflammatory and oxidative mechanisms. Anthocyanin-rich black chokeberry (Aronia melanocarpa) may influence these responses and short-term iron regulation. This study evaluated the effects of black chokeberry supplementation on iron metabolism, inflammation, antioxidant capacity, and hematological status in female competitive swimmers. METHODS: Twenty-two female swimmers (13.14 ± 1.42 years) were randomly allocated to a supplementation or placebo group. Participants completed two identical swimming tests comprising 800-, 200-, and 50-m efforts before and after 57.32 ± 8.31 days of supplementation. Blood was collected before exercise, immediately after exercise, and after 3 h of recovery. RESULTS: Most inflammatory markers showed time-dependent changes without significant group effects. C-reactive protein decreased from pre- to post-exercise during the second test in the supplemented group (p = 0.0325; Cohen's d = 1.29), whereas placebo recovery values increased between tests (p < 0.0001; Cohen's d = 3.33). Total antioxidant capacity showed a significant time × group interaction (p = 0.0007), with higher recovery values in the supplemented group. Iron, unsaturated iron-binding capacity, and total iron-binding capacity showed significant time effects (all p < 0.0001). Hepcidin also showed a significant time effect, with significant within-group increases only in the placebo group. Transferrin was lower in the supplemented group at Post II (p = 0.0071; Cohen's d = 1.17), whereas ferritin remained unchanged and hematological parameters showed no consistent between-group differences. CONCLUSION: Black chokeberry supplementation may influence markers related to short-term post-exercise iron availability, potentially in association with inflammatory and antioxidant responses, without detectable effects on body iron stores or erythropoiesis. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: The study was retrospectively registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NCT06486623; registration date: 2024-07-03).

metadata.title: Effects of Morning Strength and Power Priming Exercises on Afternoon Physical and Cognitive Performance in Male Rugby Union Players.
metadata.abstract: The objective of this study was to assess the effect of morning strength and power priming exercises on afternoon physical and cognitive performance in male rugby union players. On two occasions in a randomised, counterbalanced design, 25 male rugby union players completed morning physical (countermovement jump, 40 m linear sprint) and cognitive (rapid visual information processing; spatial working memory; paired associates of learning) assessments. Control (passive rest) or intervention (barbell back squat, 3 × 3 repetitions at 85% of one repetition maximum and barbell squat jump, 5 × 3 repetitions at 40% one repetition maximum) trials were implemented 5.5 h before afternoon assessments. Differences between morning and afternoon assessments were found in sprinting performance following intervention for 30 m fly (-0.08 ± 0.13 s, p = 0.004, ES: 0.615) and 40 m (-0.12 ± 0.17 s, p = 0.001, ES: 0.711) relative to control (0.03 ± 0.07 s, p = 0.022, ES: -0.476; 0.01 ± 0.09 s, p = 0.740, ES: -0.065, 30 m fly and 40 m, respectively). Afternoon countermovement jump flight time improved following intervention compared with control (2% vs. 0%, p = 0.012, ES: -0.53). No changes were found for cognitive assessments (p > 0.05). Morning strength and power priming exercises combining heavy-load traditional and light-load ballistic exercises effectively enhanced vertical jump and sprint performance, but not cognitive performance, in the afternoon in male rugby union players.

metadata.title: Lower Sport Nutrition Knowledge in Masters Track and Field Athletes Compared with Younger Competitors.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Appropriate nutrition is essential for supporting both athletic performance and healthy aging. In masters athletes, the physiological demands of aging and the nutritional needs of competitive sport are combined. However, dietary intakes of masters athletes do not generally meet sport nutrition recommendations. Despite evidence linking nutrition knowledge to dietary quality, sport nutrition knowledge among competitive masters athletes has not previously been evaluated. OBJECTIVES: The primary objective of this observational cross-sectional study was to assess nutrition knowledge in masters athletes competing at the World Masters Athletics Championships compared to varsity athletes with structured dietetic support. METHODS: Masters track and field athletes competing at World Masters Athletics Championships as well as varsity university track and field athletes completed the Abridged Nutrition for Sport Knowledge Questionnaire to assess both general and sport-specific nutritional knowledge. Differences in scores attained by masters and varsity athletes were assessed using independent t-tests. RESULTS: A total of 238 athletes participated (n=86 varsity athletes; n=152 masters athletes; n=120 males; n=118 females). Varsity athletes scored significantly higher on overall nutrition knowledge (51.0±12.8%) compared with masters athletes (45.2±15.0%; p=0.002). Varsity athletes also demonstrated higher scores in general nutrition (p=0.02), sport nutrition (p=0.01), and carbohydrate-related knowledge (p=0.01). No statistically significant differences were observed between groups for protein-related knowledge (p=0.09). A significant main effect of sex was observed for knowledge relating to protein, with males scoring higher than females (43.0±21.5% vs. 38.5±21.6%; p=0.039). CONCLUSIONS: Masters athletes demonstrated lower nutrition knowledge compared to varsity athletes across general and sport specific domains, with particular deficits observed in questions pertaining to carbohydrates. Given the nutritional needs of aging athletes, these gaps may contribute to the documented disconnect between dietary intake and recommendations. Tailored, evidence-based nutrition education may help improve dietary behaviors, training adaptations, and long-term health outcomes in masters athletes.

metadata.title: Orthopedic Surgeon and Primary Care Orthopedic Physician Preferences for Sports Participation for Cast-Immobilized Healing Fractures: A Survey.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: No published clinical practice guidelines outlining recommended activity restrictions were found for patients with cast-immobilized healing fractures; wide variations in practice exist. This survey aimed to elucidate physician/surgeon preferences for sports participation for patients with short arm cast-immobilized distal radial metaphyseal fractures. METHODS: Attending orthopedic surgeons, physiatrists, and primary care sports medicine physicians at a single urban tertiary-care orthopedic hospital were invited to complete an anonymous survey with up to 26 questions from 5/2023-7/2023. Descriptive statistics were done. Pearson Chi-Square tests compared pediatric surgeons to all other providers. RESULTS: One hundred twenty physicians and surgeons were invited to participate. Response rate was 43% (51/120); 59% (30/51) reported treating distal radial fractures with casting and were invited to complete the remaining survey; 70% (21/30) allow return to sports while casted. For respondents permitting sports/activity participation, factors impacting this decision included longer healing time from injury, minimal displacement, greater radiographic healing, and older age at the time of injury. Type of activity, effect on quality of life, level of competition, effect on college/team recruitment, and patient and parental pressure were noted factors impacting activity recommendations. Comparing pediatric orthopedic surgeons with all other providers, there was no notable difference in proportion permitting return to sport/activity in cast (63% vs. 73%, P = 0.67). CONCLUSION: For cast-immobilized healing fractures of the distal radius, many physicians/surgeons permit sport/activity participation in some capacity, with multiple variables impacting providers preference for activity restrictions. Clinical practice guidelines delineating activity restrictions for cast-immobilized fractures should be developed.

metadata.title: Task Force 5: Clinical Considerations for Myocarditis and Selected Cardiovascular Conditions, Including Valvular Heart Disease.
metadata.abstract: Athletes with myocarditis, pericarditis, valvular heart disease, and other acquired cardiovascular conditions require careful evaluation when considering competitive sports participation. This document outlines key clinical considerations, risk factors, and expert consensus, serving as the rationale for Section V of the recent AHA/ACC Scientific Statement: Clinical Considerations for Competitive Sports Participation for Athletes with Cardiovascular Abnormalities. Disease-specific risk stratification and shared decision-making are essential in determining return-to-play eligibility. This Task Force document addresses myocarditis, pericarditis, the cardiovascular impact of respiratory viral infections, incidental myocardial fibrosis, Kawasaki disease, infiltrative cardiomyopathies, and valvular heart disease.

metadata.title: Task Force 9: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Athletes with Cardiac Channelopathies.
metadata.abstract: Cardiac channelopathies, including long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, Brugada syndrome, and short QT syndrome, are heterogeneous conditions, which can lead to varying risks in athletes depending on their symptoms, disease severity, genotype, and therapies initiated. Historically, athletes with these conditions were excluded from participation with blanket restrictions, despite an absence of data. More recently, a number of studies have provided more scientific evidence to guide decision making and have been incorporated into these guidelines for athletes with cardiac channelopathies. Many athletes with these conditions may be supported in their decision to return to play as part of a shared decision-making model when they have been assessed, risk stratified, and appropriately treated by a specialist with expertise in these conditions.

metadata.title: Mid-term functional outcomes and graft survivorship after allograft ACL reconstruction in recreationally active adults aged 40-60 years.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: An increasing proportion of anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstructions are performed in older recreationally active adults; however, mid-term functional and graft survivorship data remain limited for this specific population. PURPOSE: To evaluate mid-term functional outcomes, return to recreational sport, and graft survivorship following primary allograft ACL reconstruction in recreationally active adults aged 40-60 years. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study included 300 recreationally active adults aged 40-60 years who underwent primary allograft ACL reconstruction between 2015 and 2019. All grafts were non-irradiated and preserved by freezing according to the tissue bank protocol. Validated patient-reported outcome measures (IKDC, KOOS, Tegner) were collected preoperatively and at final follow-up. Return to sport was defined as sustained participation in pre-injury recreational activity. Graft failure was defined by recurrent instability, imaging-confirmed rupture, or revision surgery. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to assess graft survivorship. RESULTS: At a mean follow-up of 62.4 ± 9.1 months, significant improvements were observed across all functional outcome measures. The mean IKDC score improved from 46.2 ± 11.8 preoperatively to 82.4 ± 10.6 at final follow-up, and the mean KOOS overall score increased from 58.7 ± 13.4 to 86.1 ± 9.8. Documented resumption of recreational sport participation occurred in 87.3% of patients at a mean of 8.9 ± 2.4 months postoperatively. Kaplan-Meier graft survivorship was 98.3% at 2 years, 96.7% at 3 years, and 94.8% at 5 years. Sixteen graft failures (5.3%) were recorded. CONCLUSION: In recreationally active adults aged 40-60 years, primary allograft ACL reconstruction was associated with improvement in patient-reported outcomes, frequent resumption of recreational sport participation, and satisfactory graft survivorship at mid-term follow-up. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective cohort study.

metadata.title: Updates on Low Energy Availability in Athletes: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and the Female or Male Athlete Triad.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This paper evaluates the latest literature on low energy availability (LEA) in athletes, which is the basis for the clinical conditions known as the Female Athlete Triad, Male Athlete Triad, and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). It explores how these different conditions are related, and how the clinician can approach screening, diagnosis, and management of LEA in athletes. RECENT FINDINGS: Within the past five years the Male Athlete Triad Consensus Statements were published in 2021, expanding upon knowledge regarding LEA in the Female Athlete Triad and applying this to the male population. Additionally, there has been an important update to the REDs model and a new clinical assessment tool (CAT2) published in 2023. This is based on new research into the different physiologic and psychologic sequelae of LEA. This has sparked additional discussion regarding the diagnosis, management, and prevention of LEA. The consequences of LEA can be severe, and can affect multiple different organ systems. Treatment should ideally involve a multidisciplinary team consisting of a physician, dietitian, and mental health provider, but may also include additional professionals such as athletic trainers, physical therapists, physiologists, other medical specialists, or other members of the athlete support system (including family and coaches). The mainstay of management remains optimizing energy availability (EA) through improving macro and micronutrient intake, and also requires addressing some of the more common sequelae of LEA. Prevention largely focuses on educational efforts and fostering healthy environments, particularly when discussing weight, body composition, and performance.

metadata.title: Dyslipidemia management in athletes: A comparative commentary on the 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline and contemporary sports cardiology recommendations.
metadata.abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the leading cause of exercise-related sudden cardiac death in athletes older than 35 years, and dyslipidemia is one of its principal modifiable drivers. The 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Blood Cholesterol introduces several advances directly relevant to athletes, including restored LDL-C treatment targets, universal lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] measurement, the PREVENT-ASCVD risk equations, expanded options for selective coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring, and a more aggressive approach to lipid-lowering therapy (LLT). However, sports cardiology guidelines and consensus statements offer important caveats that must be reconciled with these general-population recommendations: existing risk calculators, including PREVENT, do not reliably estimate cardiovascular risk in athletes, and routine CAC scoring is not recommended in athletes at low calculated risk. This commentary compares and contrasts general-population dyslipidemia recommendations with athlete-specific guidance from contemporary sports cardiology consensus documents, highlights recent evidence on Lp(a), wearable-derived training load, and risk score performance across the physical activity spectrum, and proposes a five-step clinical framework, refined to reflect athlete-specific risk stratification, for dyslipidemia evaluation and management in this population.

metadata.title: Changes in Hormone Cycles and Exercise Capacity During Testosterone Therapy in a Transmasculine Triathlete: A Case Study.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The impact of testosterone therapy on the hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiology of transmasculine individuals is not well understood. Existing studies report limited metrics at large time intervals between data collection points. METHODS: High-resolution temporal data were collected from a single amateur trans male triathlete over 13 months-including one baseline month and 12 months on testosterone therapy-to characterize hormone, strength, body composition, aerobic, and training load profiles. RESULTS: Daily urine hormone monitoring revealed that progesterone and luteinizing hormone are the clearest metrics associated with cessation of menses. After 1 yr, the participant increased lean body mass by 12%, average hand grip strength by 16%, jump height by 16%, and average knee isometric strength by 18%, but did not lose fat mass or show changes in isokinetic knee strength. Fluctuations in running fitness and maximum oxygen consumption ( V ˙ O 2 m a x ) were associated with both training and testosterone levels, with future work needed to untangle their relative contributions. CONCLUSION: This study provides the most comprehensive characterization of the impacts of testosterone therapy on hormone cycles, exercise capacity, and physiological changes in a single person to date, as well as observations to help inform the design of larger cohort studies.

metadata.title: Interatrial Septal Disorders are Independently Associated with Delayed Post-Exercise Heart Rate Recovery in Athletes.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Interatrial septal disorders (IASD) are among the most common congenital cardiac anomalies. Their impact on cardiac autonomic function in athletes remains poorly defined. In this study, we aimed to evaluate the prevalence of IASD and their association with cardiac autonomic function, assessed by heart rate recovery (HRR), in a cohort of adult athletes. METHODS: This cross-sectional study enrolled 1,018 adult athletes undergoing pre-participation cardiovascular screening at the Exercise and Sports Medicine Unit of ''A. Cardarelli'' Hospital, Campobasso, Italy, between January 2024 and May 2025. Trans-thoracic echocardiography with contrast imaging was performed to diagnose IASD. HRR was assessed during exercise stress testing using the Modified Bruce Protocol. ΔHRR was calculated as the change from peak heart rate during exercise to that measured during 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th minutes of recovery. RESULTS: IASD were identified in 331 athletes (32.5%), including patent foramen ovale (12.5%), redundant interatrial septum (21.7%), atrial septal aneurysm (3.3%), and ostium secundum (1.7%). Athletes with IASD exhibited significantly lower ΔHRR at 1 min (30.8 ± 13.9 vs. 39.9 ± 18.1 bpm, p < 0.001) and 2 min (61.0 ± 17.9 vs. 66.1 ± 16.7 bpm, p < 0.001) post-exercise. On multivariable regression, IASD was the strongest independent predictor of impaired ΔHRR 1 (β =- 11.19, p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: IASD are prevalent in athletes and independently associated with delayed post-exercise early HRR, suggesting an impairment in post-exercise vagal reactivation.

metadata.title: Beyond Morphology: Quantitative Bilateral Self-Referenced Frequency-Domain Diffuse Optical Spectroscopy Reveals Functional Abnormalities in Patellar Tendinopathy.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Patellar tendinopathy (PT) involves functional and metabolic abnormalities that may precede structural degeneration, whereas MRI and ultrasonography primarily depict morphology. To bridge this gap, we aim to develop a quantitative optical method for detecting PT-related functional and hemodynamic abnormalities. METHODS: We developed an embedded multi-wavelength frequency-domain diffuse optical spectroscopy system integrating sinusoidal modulation, synchronized acquisition, real-time Goertzel demodulation, optical-property inversion, chromophore fitting, and standardized grid scanning over the patellar tendon region. To reduce inter-subject variability, a bilateral self-referenced strategy used the contralateral tendon as an endogenous reference. A composite optical biomarker, Tendon Hemodynamic Index (THI), was defined by integrating differential tissue oxygenation and blood-volume-related information. RESULTS: Phantom and in vivo measurements demonstrated robust quantitative performance. In a clinical cohort, THI was significantly elevated in PT patients and correlated with symptom severity and functional impairment across the full cohort, with Spearman correlations of 0.69 with the Numeric Rating Scale and -0.74 with the Victorian Institute of Sport Assessment-Patella score. In this exploratory cohort, THI distinguished PT from healthy controls with 91.8% accuracy, 95.8% sensitivity, 88.0% specificity, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.928. In imaging negative but symptom-positive cases, THI achieved 88.2% classification accuracy. In three exploratory follow-up cases, THI decreased toward the bilateral baseline as symptoms improved over 8 weeks. CONCLUSION: The proposed method enables self-referenced quantification of PT-related functional abnormalities. SIGNIFICANCE: By revealing tendon hemodynamic abnormalities beyond structural imaging, this work supports early PT detection, objective severity assessment, and quantitative monitoring of disease recovery.

metadata.title: Warning signs of Injury: Changes in pain, training load, and wellness in elite youth athletes.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Examine week-by-week changes during the four weeks preceding injury compared with injury-free weeks. DESIGN: Prospective study. SETTING: and main outcome: Training load was calculated as (weekly training minutes x average weekly rate of perceived exertion)/1000 (sRPE). Pain was assessed with a rating scale 0-10. Wellness (sleep, fatigue, stress and mental recovery) were standardized using Z-scores. Injury was self-reported. PARTICIPANTS: Elite youth athletes. RESULTS: Among 146 athletes, 118 (80.8%) reported 125 injuries. Mean age was 17.0 (SD 0.8). Compared with injury-free weeks, significantly higher pain scores were observed one (md [IQR]: 2.0 [0.0-4.0], p = 0.039) and two weeks (2.0 [1.0-3.0], p = 0.047) prior to injury. Median sRPE was significantly lower three (md [IQR]: 2.30 [0.75-4.20], p = 0.012) and four weeks (2.40 [0.96-3.96], p = 0.011). Sleep, stress and total wellness were significantly lower one week (mean [SD]: -0.348 [1.1], p = 0.004; -0.272 [0.9], p = 0.017; -0.244 [1.0], p = 0.011), while stress also showed reduction two weeks prior to injury (-0.244 [1.0], p = 0.042). CONCLUSION: Changes were observed mainly in the week preceding injury. Increased pain and reduced wellness may serve as early warning signs, while decreased training load may reflect adaptation rather than causation. These findings support injury as a progressive process with detectable warning signs.

metadata.title: Thumb muscle activation with task-specific exercise: A pilot study with participant self-report implementation outcomes.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Thumb carpometacarpal osteoarthritis is a common source of pain, weakness, and reduced hand function and upper extremity rehabilitation. Although isometric stabilization exercises are commonly used in hand therapy to support dynamic thumb carpometacarpal control, limited task-specific evidence guides exercise selection. PURPOSE: To examine muscle activation across four isometric thumb-hand positions in healthy adults and describe participant perceptions of the protocol's acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness before testing in symptomatic hand therapy samples. STUDY DESIGN: Cross-sectional, within-subject repeated-measures pilot study. METHODS: Seven healthy right-handed adults (mean age, 22.7 ± 0.48 years) performed four submaximal isometric exercise conditions at approximately 80% perceived effort: composite finger-thumb squeeze, "bunny-ears" pinch, resisted index-finger abduction, and fingertip-only press. Surface electromyography was recorded from the abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, first dorsal interosseous, and forearm flexor group. Integrated electromyography was normalized within participants to each muscle's maximum response across conditions. A two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance (condition × muscle) compared normalized activation. Participants rated acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness on five-point Likert scales. RESULTS: Normalized activation differed by muscle, F(3,18) = 14.22, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.70, with a significant condition × muscle interaction, F(9,54) = 7.29, p < 0.001, ηp² = 0.55. Abductor pollicis brevis activation was highest during composite squeeze and bunny-ears pinch (0.93 ± 0.05 and 0.85 ± 0.06) and lowest during resisted index-finger abduction (0.31 ± 0.07). Opponens pollicis activation was highest during composite squeeze and resisted index-finger abduction (0.79 ± 0.07 and 0.75 ± 0.09). Mean construct-based ratings of acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness ranged from 4.54-4.79 out of 5. CONCLUSIONS: Findings provide preliminary evidence to inform hand therapy exercise selection by showing that functional isometric thumb-hand positions produce distinct intrinsic and extrinsic activation profiles. Favorable participant perceptions support protocol refinement and testing in larger and symptomatic hand therapy samples.

metadata.title: Lower extremity joint biomechanics from a single crossover drop task demonstrate superior predictive potential for secondary ACL injuries than drop vertical jump or single leg landing tasks.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Secondary anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injuries remain a significant concern after return-to-sport (RTS) following ACL reconstruction (ACLR), with rates as high as 24%. Identifying biomechanical predictors of re-injury is critical for improving RTS protocols. PURPOSE: To compare the predictive potential of three common landing tasks [drop vertical jump (DVJ), single-leg landing (SLL), and single-leg crossover drop (SCD)] for secondary ACL injury risk in post-ACLR athletes. METHODS: A multicenter cohort of 150 athletes (age 13-30 years) that were cleared for RTS post-ACLR completed DVJ, SLL, and SCD tasks during 3D motion analysis; 144 athletes data met criteria for analysis. Peak kinematic and kinetic variables (n = 126) were analyzed using a penalized logistic regression with an elastic net penalty. Predictive models were evaluated via ROC curves, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values. RESULTS: The SCD task demonstrated the strongest predictive performance for secondary ACL injury, with a validated positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.57, negative predictive value (NPV) of 0.96, sensitivity of 80.0%, specificity of 88.9%, and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.933. The DVJ demonstrated moderate predictive performance (PPV=0.43, NPV=0.92, sensitivity=60.0%, specificity=85.7%, AUC=0.843), while the SLL demonstrated the lowest performance (PPV=0.33, NPV=0.92, sensitivity=60.0%, specificity=78.6%, AUC=0.736). CONCLUSION: Lower extremity biomechanics during SCD provide greater predictive performance for secondary ACL injury compared with the DVJ or SLL. The findings suggest that SCD captures biomechanical characteristics relevant to secondary ACL injury risk and may improve identification of athletes at elevated risk following ACL reconstruction. However, further validation and model simplification are needed before clinical implementation as a stand-alone screening tool.

metadata.title: Increases in Agility and Quantitative Movement Quality Following a Coach-Led, Basketball-Specific Neuromuscular Training Warm-Up Programme in Adolescent Athletes.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Coach-led, basketball-specific neuromuscular training (NMT) warm-up programs have been shown to reduce injury risk. However, changes in agility and movement quality following such NMT in high school basketball players are not well characterized. METHODS: In this pre-experimental study, high school basketball players (42 males, 31 females, 16 ± 1.4 years) performed a 10-minute, coach-led, basketball-specific NMT warm-up programme before practices and games (10-14 weeks). Changes in the Lane Agility Test (LAT) and single-leg squat (SLS) kinematics, encompassing trunk, pelvis, hip, and lower extremity kinematics and a composite score (SLS Score), from pre-to post-intervention were assessed. Relationships between pre-intervention scores, sex, the number of NMT sessions completed, and outcomes were assessed with linear regressions. RESULTS: LAT completion times decreased following the NMT intervention, with larger changes associated with slower pre-intervention scores and more completed NMT sessions. SLS Scores were higher after the NMT intervention, potentially attributable to better pelvic and hip kinematics. CONCLUSIONS: In this single-arm preliminary and exploratory study, favourable changes in agility and SLS kinematics following a coach-led, basketball-specific NMT programme were observed, with preliminary evidence of a dose-response relationship for agility. However, this study was non-randomized and lacked a control group. Therefore, these results should not be interpreted to suggest a causal relationship between the NMT performed and the changes in outcomes. In addition to NMT's role in injury prevention, coaches and players should be cognizant about performance and movement quality changes potentially associated with this accessible version of NMT.

metadata.title: Clinical validation of a vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge plasma activation device for plasma-activated platelet-rich plasma preparation in osteoarthritis pain management.
metadata.abstract: Cold atmospheric plasma (CAP) has significant potential in biomedical applications. However, conventional plasma activation requires electrodes to contact a liquid directly, exposing it to the external environment. This conflicts with sterile, closed preparations required clinically. A vial wall-based dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma activation device addresses this need by using standard clinical blood collection tube walls as a dielectric barrier. Electrodes contact only the tube exterior, never the liquid inside, and activation requires simply inserting the tube into the reactor chamber. Applied to platelet-rich plasma (PRP) therapy for osteoarthritis (OA), the device produced plasma-activated PRP (PA-PRP) with enhanced platelet activation, increased levels of transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β; 24%), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF; 37%), and insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1; 32%), and broadly upregulated anti-inflammatory cytokines. In the destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) mouse OA model, PA-PRP treatment was associated with improved gait parameters and lower cartilage degeneration scores relative to PRP treatment. Human OA cartilage explants showed greater matrix staining after PA-PRP treatment. In an exploratory, randomized, single-blind split-body study involving three patients, PA-PRP-treated knees, compared with contralateral PRP-treated knees, showed numerically larger improvements in visual analog scale (VAS) pain score, Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) score, and effusion volume at week 15, with no adverse events during observation. These clinical observations are descriptive and hypothesis-generating, as the sample size precludes reliable efficacy or comparative safety inferences. Together, findings support device feasibility and PA-PRP use in OA and provide a rationale for adequately powered studies.

metadata.title: From suspension to clearance: return-to-fight decision-making after concussion and knockout in combat sports-a critical review.
metadata.abstract: Combat-sport medical suspensions restrict participation after knockout, head-blow stoppage, or suspected concussion. Expiry of a suspension does not establish clinical recovery or replace required medical clearance. This critical narrative review examines how suspension rules, concussion care, and graded return to training can be coordinated in boxing and related combat sports. We critically integrated international concussion consensus, combat-sport guidance, official regulations, and selected rehabilitation and epidemiological studies. The reviewed guidance already combines time restrictions with medical requirements; differences concern duration, permitted activities, assessment criteria, and implementation. General concussion principles apply irrespective of whether the injury-producing contact was intentional. Early light physical activity and prescribed aerobic exercise must be distinguished from later sport-specific activity and renewed head-impact risk. We propose a framework with three dimensions-clinical recovery, regulatory eligibility, and functional progression-and three decision gates. Gate A is medical authorization for activity carrying head-impact risk; Gate B is expiry of the applicable no-contact restriction. Both are prerequisites for contact progression. Gate C permits competition only after the required training progression, expiry of the competition suspension, and final medical authorization. Clinicians determine medical readiness; coaches and rehabilitation staff support graded training within those limits. The dimensions may overlap, but contact progression follows Gates A and B and competition follows Gate C. Priorities are clearer activity definitions, consistent documentation of clearance, adherence to existing requirements, longitudinal records, and prospective evaluation. This framework is an unvalidated implementation proposal rather than a new clearance test or a universal suspension timetable.

metadata.title: Within-player load-wellness monitoring and lower-limb pain in elite female football: A reproducible secondary analysis of the SoccerMon dataset.
metadata.abstract: Routine athlete-monitoring data can test whether within-player changes in training load and wellness precede health problems, but sparse outcomes and incomplete reporting complicate inference. We conducted a reproducible secondary longitudinal analysis of the public SoccerMon dataset, comprising 50 players from two Norwegian elite women's football teams monitored in 2020-2021. The outcome was onset on day t (the index player-day) of a self-reported lower-limb pain/injury episode after a 7-day episode washout. The primary risk set contained 42 onset-days from 15 players; the complete-case soreness interaction analysis contained 28 onset-days from nine event players. Under retrospective full-period within-player standardization, the focal acute-load x soreness interaction was estimated below 1.0 by Firth logistic regression (odds ratio [OR] 0.63, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.45-0.97), but uncertainty remained substantial. When within-player standardization was recalculated using only observations available before each day, the interaction attenuated to OR 0.97 (0.73-1.25). These data therefore do not provide stable evidence that within-player load deviations or load x wellness interactions are associated with next-day self-reported lower-limb pain onset. Sparse events, event concentration, missing monitoring data, and team/season imbalance further limit precision. In practice, daily load and wellness signals should be interpreted as contextual longitudinal information rather than as stand-alone next-day risk thresholds.

metadata.title: Autologous Osteochondral Transplantation Remains a Reliable Option for Talar Osteochondral Lesions, With Low Knee Donor-Site Morbidity.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Autologous osteochondral transplantation (AOT) is a surgical option for talar osteochondral lesions (OCL), with favorable outcomes and high return-to-sport rates; however, knee donor-site morbidity remains a concern. PURPOSE: To evaluate clinical and functional outcomes, complications, return to work and sport, and satisfaction after AOT for talar OCL. STUDY DESIGN: Retrospective case series. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients ≥18 years with talar OCL treated with AOT (2011-2022; minimum 2-year follow-up); patients with prior knee pain or surgery, infection, advanced osteoarthritis, or rheumatologic disease were excluded. Outcomes included the AOFAS hindfoot, Lysholm, and Tegner scores, ankle and knee visual analog scale (VAS) pain, satisfaction, return to work and sport, and complications. RESULTS: Thirty-seven patients (78% male; median age, 36 years; median follow-up, 24 months) were included. Median lesion size was 150 mm², all medial; 14 (38%) had concomitant procedures. The AOFAS score improved from 54.5 to 95.8 (mean difference, 41.3; 95% CI, 38.4-44.3) and ankle VAS from 7.0 to 1.6 (-5.4; 95% CI, -5.9 to -4.9) (both p < 0.001). Postoperative Lysholm score was 98.8 ± 4.0 and knee VAS 1.2 ± 0.8 (no preoperative knee scores). Return to work took 2.3 ± 1.2 months; all 32 athletes resumed sport at 6.5 ± 2.1 months, 20 (63%) in their pre-injury sport. Tegner scores were unchanged (5.4 vs 5.5; p = 0.624). One knee hemarthrosis and one repeat ankle arthroscopy occurred. CONCLUSIONS: AOT for talar OCL yielded favorable short-term outcomes, high return-to-work and return-to-sport rates, and low reported knee donor-site morbidity; baseline knee scores were unavailable. LEVEL OF CLINICAL EVIDENCE: 4.

metadata.title: An Adaptive Knee Brace Is Associated With Improved Dynamic Stabilization Compared With a Standard Passive Brace in Anterior Cruciate Ligament-Deficient Men During a Functional Hop Task.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: To compare the dynamic knee stabilization effects of an adaptive dynamic brace (ADB) with those of a standard passive brace in anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)-deficient men. METHODS: ACL-deficient participants were included. The subjects performed 3 single-leg functional hop tests: drop jump, crossover hop, and 90° rotational hop. Each task was performed once while wearing the ADB and once while wearing a traditional passive brace. Three-dimensional kinematic data were collected using an 8-camera optoelectronic motion-capture system. Repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to evaluate the effects of brace condition and time. An a priori power analysis indicated that a minimum of 12 participants were required. RESULTS: Twelve ACL-deficient participants were included (age: 30.2 ± 3.4 years; time since injury: 32 ± 6 months; ACL-Return to Sport after Injury score: 70 ± 3). No significant differences in knee flexion angles were observed between braces. Knee flexion during landing was significantly lower in the crossover hop compared with the drop jump and rotational hop tasks (P < .01). During the drop jump task, the ADB significantly reduced knee valgus angles (P < .01). In the crossover hop task, the ADB significantly reduced both knee valgus and rotational angles (P < .01). During the rotational hop task, a significant brace-by-time interaction was observed for knee valgus (P < .05) and rotational angles (P < .05). CONCLUSIONS: The ADB showed improved dynamic stabilization particularly during high-risk landing and rotational movement compared with a standard passive brace. CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The ADB may enhance the effectiveness of rehabilitation strategies in ACL-deficient individuals by improving dynamic knee stability during functional activities.

metadata.title: Vitamin D Insufficiency as a Nutritional Stress Amplifier: An Evidence-Weighted Framework for Adaptive Reserve under Exercise and Energy-Deficit Stress.
metadata.abstract: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid whose biological activity depends on conversion of circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D into calcitriol, the active ligand of the vitamin D receptor. Although vitamin D has often been discussed as a potential ergogenic nutrient, evidence for direct performance-enhancing effects in athletes remains inconsistent. This review proposes that vitamin D insufficiency, used here as a context-dependent descriptive label for low circulating 25(OH)D rather than as a universal diagnostic category, may function as a nutritional stress amplifier that narrows adaptive reserve when mechanical, energetic, endocrine, inflammatory, and neuroendocrine stressors converge. The strongest evidence derives from the vitamin D-calcium-phosphate-PTH-FGF23 axis, through which calcitriol-VDR signaling supports mineral homeostasis, skeletal remodeling, and resilience to repetitive skeletal loading. Emerging evidence suggests intersections with skeletal muscle repair, myokine and osteokine signaling, inflammatory regulation, and tissue adaptation, although athlete-specific validation is needed. Low energy availability and Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport provide a translational model in which low circulating 25(OH)D may become more relevant because multiple nutritional, endocrine, skeletal, and recovery stressors coexist. Brain-related pathways involving fatigue, sleep, HPA-axis-related recovery, BDNF, monoaminergic signaling, and interoceptive processing are retained only as hypothesis-generating domains, not as evidence that vitamin D status modifies cognition, mood, motivation, behavior, or central recovery mechanisms in athletes. Future studies should move beyond static 25-hydroxyvitamin D assessment and unstratified supplementation trials toward dynamic stress-recovery phenotyping. This framework positions low circulating 25(OH)D status as a testable conditional modifier of stress-recovery trajectories rather than an isolated determinant of athletic performance or a primary clinical target.

metadata.title: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport and its Implications for the Foot and Ankle Surgeon.
metadata.abstract: Relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) is a syndrome caused by low energy availability that affects multiple physiologic systems in both male and female athletes. Stress fractures of the foot and ankle are often the first signs of RED-S; therefore, it is crucial that orthopedic surgeons are aware of and able to identify this disorder. This article focuses on RED-S and provides a framework for understanding the disorder, it's relevancy to the orthopedic foot and ankle surgeon, and offers suggestions for diagnostic strategies and treatment approaches that are imperative for safe return to play.

metadata.title: Sports-Related Back Pain and Injuries: From Muscle Strain to Spondylolisthesis.
metadata.abstract: Back pain is common in both the general population and young athletes, with risk increasing in sports that involve repetitive extension, rotation, and axial loading. Although most cases resolve with time, accurate diagnosis is essential to distinguish common musculoskeletal causes from more serious conditions. This article reviews key causes of athletic back pain, including muscle strain, mechanical low back pain, spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis, lumbar disc herniation, and sacroiliac joint dysfunction. It also examines diagnosis, treatment, and return to play considerations. Early recognition and appropriate management help ensure a safe and timely return to sport.

metadata.title: Anatomic Triple-Bundle Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Technique With Three Femoral Tunnels and Three Tibial Tunnels Using Hamstring Tendon.
metadata.abstract: Reconstruction of the anterior cruciate ligament is a common procedure for athletes with the aim of returning to sports activities. Despite improved surgical techniques and rehabilitation, the return-to-sport rate and retear rates remain unsatisfactory. We described a technique for triple-bundle anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction with three femur tunnels and three tibial tunnels using hamstring tendon.

metadata.title: Clinical Assessments to Inform Return to Play Prognosis Following Acute Hamstring Injury: An Evidence-Informed Guide for Clinicians.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Rehabilitation clinicians aim to provide a return to play (RTP) prognosis following acute hamstring injury based on various clinical assessments, including subjective interview questions and physical examinations. CLINICAL QUESTION: What subjective interview questions and physical examinations should be prioritised during an initial clinical assessment following acute hamstring injury to inform RTP? KEY RESULTS: There are key subjective interview questions and physical examination findings to inform RTP prognosis following acute hamstring injury. Prolonged RTP time has been associated with athletes who: 1) recall higher pain ratings at the time of injury; 2) report pain with palpation closer to the ischial tuberosity; 3) have greater cranio-caudal length of palpable pain; 4) present with between-leg deficits of greater magnitude in maximal hip flexion active knee extension range of motion and isometric knee flexion strength in outer-range (supine with 90° hip/knee flexion) and/or mid-range (prone with 0° hip and ~15° knee flexion); and 4) experience pain during outer-range hamstring contraction. CLINICAL APPLICATION: This evidence-informed clinical commentary may help clinicians prioritise subjective interview questions and physical examinations to inform their RTP prognosis following acute hamstring injury.
