metadata.title: Ask the experts: a practitioner-centred approach to resilience in emergency medical services.
metadata.abstract: Background: Resilience in high-stress occupations is commonly framed as a trait, an outcome, or the absence of psychopathology. None of these framings captures what practitioners in emergency medical services actually do, and interventions built on trait-based models have produced weak or inconsistent effects.Objective: This study argues that frontline resilience in emergency medical services is better understood as a domain-specific expert skill, and that work mode - a deliberately entered state, akin to an athlete's game face, in which the demands of the task rather than the emotional force of the scene govern functioning - is its central empirical signature. The aims were to identify factors that intensify traumatic impact, characterise the strategies practitioners use to maintain functioning, and explore systemic and relational barriers that constrain coping.Method: Twenty Queensland Ambulance Service paramedics and dispatchers (tenure 2-38 years) participated in semi-structured interviews, analysed via reflexive thematic analysis.Results: Three intensifiers of traumatic impact (unpredictability, moral weight, personal threat) defined the operational demands against which resilience was enacted. Three coping themes (baseline buffers, work mode, social scaffolding) described the architecture of sustained functioning. Work mode exhibited the defining features of skilled performance: domain specificity, a phased temporal structure (preparation, containment, recovery), and a developmental trajectory from effortful to automatic execution. Two further themes (organisational distrust, the outsider gap) described the systemic and relational conditions that constrain coping.Conclusions: Treating resilience as expertise shifts the field from descriptive stressor-outcome accounts towards assessable, trainable capacities, and exposes the limitations of trait-based self-report measures that cannot distinguish genuine resilience from unsustainable stoicism.

metadata.title: High Survival and Continued Sports Participation After Arthroscopy for Femoroacetabular Impingement in Athletes With and Without Lateral Rim Dysplasia With Minimum 4.5-Year Follow-Up.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: To quantify the outcomes, including sporting capability, of hip arthroscopy (HA) in athletes for femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) in the presence of concomitant lateral rim dysplasia (LR-Dysplasia) compared with a matched athletic control group. METHODS: Athletes undergoing unilateral primary HA for FAI with or without LR-Dysplasia between January 2009 and May 2020 were considered. All athletes with a lateral center-edge angle of <25° on anteroposterior view were matched to those with normal overcoverage (lateral center-edge angle >30°). Patients were contacted a minimum of 4.5 years after the procedure. Outcomes included survival (avoidance of total hip replacement), revision HA, and patient-reported outcomes (PROMs) consisting of the modified Harris Hip Score (mHHS), University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) activity score, 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36), and Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC). Substantial clinical benefit thresholds were determined for each PROM, and the proportion of cases achieving substantial clinical benefit was compared between groups. Finally, the ability to continue to play sports and satisfaction were determined. RESULTS: Forty-eight patients with LR-Dysplasia were matched to 97 controls with a mean follow-up of 72 ± 19 months (54-120 months). At follow-up, survival was 100% in the LR-Dysplasia group versus 99% in controls. The revision HA rates were 6% in LR-Dysplasia patients and 9% in controls. Both groups showed significant improvements in PROMs. In the LR-Dysplasia group, mHHS improved from 82 to 100 (P < .001), UCLA from 8 to 9 (P = .114), SF-36 from 74 to 87 (P = .002), and WOMAC from 15 to 2 (P < .001). In the control group, mHHS improved from 82 to 96 (P < .001), UCLA from 7 to 10 (P = .003), SF-36 from 72 to 89 (P < .001), and WOMAC from 17 to 4 (P = .005). Between-group comparisons showed no significant differences in pre- or postoperative mHHS (P = .498; P = .183), UCLA (P = .684; P = .388), SF-36 (P = .487; P = .602), or WOMAC (P = .814; P = .390). Substantial clinical benefit was achieved by most patients for each PROM and similar between groups (P > .05 for all). No significant differences were observed between groups in PROMs or overall satisfaction with surgery (P > .05 for all). Sports participation at 5 years was 84% in the LR-Dysplasia group and 90% in controls (P = .103). CONCLUSIONS: In the absence of arthritic changes, athletes treated with arthroscopy for FAI where LR-Dysplasia is present showed high survival rates and improved pain and function. Furthermore, most athletes can maintain their preoperative levels of sport. Importantly, the outcomes observed in this specific patient cohort are comparable to those seen in athletes with normal acetabular coverage, indicating that the presence of LR-Dysplasia does not compromise the effectiveness of arthroscopic intervention for FAI in athletes. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, therapeutic retrospective comparative study.

metadata.title: Collective case study on periodized training in elite female middle- and long-distance swimmers preparing for national competition.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Elite swimmers increasingly face calendars requiring multiple performance peaks within a single season, a scenario for which traditional single-target periodization models may be insufficient. METHODS: This longitudinal collective case study followed five elite female middle- and long-distance freestyle swimmers across a 52-week macrocycle preparing for two national championships. The program combined three altitude camps, sea-level integration phases and two timed tapers. Training intensity distribution (TID) was quantified with a three-zone lactate-threshold model; hemoglobin, hematocrit, red blood cell count, creatine kinase and cortisol were measured at four time points; and performance was assessed by time-trial and official competition results. Given N = 5, analysis prioritized a smallest-worthwhile-change (SWC) classification for performance and paired effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals for blood markers rather than null-hypothesis significance testing. Hematological outcomes are concentration-based indices; training-load descriptors refer to in-water swimming only. RESULTS: Applying an SWC of ≈0.24% to the 20 athlete-by-event observations, 12/20 (60%) changes at Competition 1 and 18/20 (90%) at Competition 2 exceeded the SWC, most representing improvement over baseline; this ordering held across the full defensible range of reference variability (SWC 0.22-0.42%). Hematological effect sizes were largest at Week 27 (RBC: Hedges' g = 2.32, 95% CI [0.64, 4.01]; HCT: g = 2.04 [0.50, 3.58]), while creatine kinase and cortisol peaked at Week 17 and were closer to baseline at Week 49, compatible with a lower physiological stress state at that sampled time point. TID shifted across phases (pyramidal during base development, polarized during altitude blocks, threshold-oriented during race-pace sharpening), with marked inter-individual heterogeneity in performance and physiological responses. CONCLUSION: Across this double-peak macrocycle, most athlete-by-event changes exceeded the SWC, and the proportion doing so was higher at the second championship than at the first; these changes occurred alongside altitude-associated increases in concentration-based oxygen-transport indices and a taper-associated normalization of creatine kinase and cortisol. With no control group or randomization, only five athletes and four blood samples, several simultaneous interventions and unmeasured confounders (iron status, menstrual-cycle phase, dryland load), these findings describe associations only. They are offered as exploratory, hypothesis-generating observations from a single elite squad rather than as causal evidence.

metadata.title: Open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense: inter-day reliability and normative profiles in male contact sport athletes.
metadata.abstract: The purpose was to determine inter-day reliability and normative values for open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense (JPS). Male contact and collision sport athletes (18-40 years) participated in two study phases. Sixteen athletes completed open- and closed-chain JPS tests on two occasions (2-9 days apart) to determine inter-day reliability. Twenty-eight athletes completed the same protocol on one occasion to establish normative profiles. Open-chain JPS was assessed in a standing position using shoulder flexion to pre-defined angles with a laser pointer (55°, 90° and 125° of humerothoracic flexion; no haptic target); closed-chain JPS was assessed in a push-up position by reproducing target positions (chest lowered onto a hurdle at 16.5 cm [low] or 30.5 cm [high]; an initial haptic target). Three-dimensional kinematics quantified repositioning errors. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and standard error of measurement (SEM) were calculated for reliability. Pearson correlations were calculated between open and closed-chain errors. Open-chain tests demonstrated moderate reliability across both arms (ICCs = 0.71-0.74), with better reliability on the dominant limb (ICCs = 0.68-0.90) compared to the non-dominant (ICCs = 0.43-0.55). SEM values ranged from 0.70 to 2.03°. Closed-chain tests showed poor reliability at the high target (ICC = 0.49) but good reliability at the low target (ICC = 0.81, SEM = 10.2 mm). Normative data indicated greater repositioning errors at low targets in open-chain tasks and at high targets in closed-chain tasks. Correlations between open- and closed-chain errors were weak to absent. Open-chain JPS testing demonstrated acceptable reliability, whereas closed-chain reliability was dependent on target height. The two tasks appear to assess distinct aspects of proprioception. The open-chain test reflects predominantly single-joint (glenohumeral) position sense, whereas the closed-chain test reflects multi-joint, composite position sense. These findings establish initial reference values for JPS in male contact athletes.

metadata.title: Comparative Plasma Proteomics of Arabian and Thoroughbred Racehorses at Rest and During Early Recovery from Training and Racing.
metadata.abstract: Breed-associated differences in the plasma proteome of Arabian and Thoroughbred racehorses at rest and during early recovery from training and racing remain incompletely characterised. Tandem mass tag (TMT)-based liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) plasma proteomics was performed on samples from 43 Thoroughbred and Arabian racehorses collected at rest and 30-40min post-exercise during early-season training, mid-season training, and racing. Breed and sex effects were tested with false discovery rate correction within each contrast and an effect-size threshold (absolute fold change >= 1.20); age and race placing were evaluated by breed- and time-specific Spearman correlations. More proteins met the reporting criteria for between-breed differences during initial training and racing than during mid-season training. Across the analysed contrasts, proteins with higher relative abundance in Arabians included FETUB, CNTN1, FGFR1, HGFAC and C4BPA, while proteins with lower abundance included ENPP5, SMPDL3B, KRT8 and KRT19. Age was associated with the plasma abundance of proteins annotated to coagulation, lipid transport, immune regulation and extracellular matrix-related functions. More proteins met the reporting criteria for sex-associated differences at rest than during early recovery. Exploratory associations with race placing were detected for two proteins in Thoroughbreds after exercise, with none meeting the reporting criteria in Arabians. These findings identify breed-associated plasma protein differences and candidates for independent validation.

metadata.title: Associations between countermovement jump impulse and running kinetics following ACL reconstruction.
metadata.abstract: Persistent deficits in lower-limb loading are commonly observed following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and may influence running biomechanics. Countermovement jump (CMJ) impulse can provide a phase-specific measure of force-time characteristics to reflect limb loading capacity; however, its relationship with running kinetics remains unclear. This study aimed to quantify phase-specific CMJ impulse following ACLR and examine associations with vertical ground reaction force (vGRF) metrics during treadmill running at the return-to-running phase. Forty-two participants performed three unilateral and bilateral CMJs on dual force plates and ran at 8 km/hr on an instrumented treadmill. Concentric, eccentric braking, and landing impulses were calculated. Running variables included weight acceptance rate, weight acceptance peak force, and maximum applied force. Inter-limb differences were assessed using Wilcoxon/paired t-tests. Impulse-vGRF relationships were analysed using Pearson/Spearman correlations and multiple linear regression. The ACLR limb exhibited significant deficits across all unilateral and bilateral CMJ phases, except for unilateral landing impulse. Deficits were greatest for unilateral concentric impulse (Δ1.3Ns·kg-0.67, d = 1.49, p < 0.001). Maximum applied force limb symmetry index (LSI) was explained by unilateral concentric impulse LSI (adjusted R2 = 0.25, p < 0.001). Maximum applied force of the affected limb was explained by unilateral concentric impulse (adjusted R2 = 0.38, p < 0.001). Weight acceptance peak force of the affected limb was explained by unilateral concentric and landing impulses (adjusted R2 = 0.37, p < 0.001). No meaningful relationships were observed for eccentric impulses or weight acceptance rate metrics. These findings indicate that jump impulse testing may provide clinically relevant indicators of running kinetics.

metadata.title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
metadata.abstract: Campos, BT, Rodrigues, JGdS, Cal Abad, CC, Bachi, ALL, dos Santos, CMM, Tritto, AC, Kons, RL, Penna, EM, and Prado, LS. Performance and physiological responses to strength training programs in elite judo athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study compared the effects of 2 short-term strength training models, block planning (BP) and undulating planning (UP), on performance, physiological, and perceptual responses in elite judo athletes. We hypothesized that BP would induce greater physiological strain due to the concentration of training stimuli. Eighteen judokas (14 men and 4 women) were randomly assigned to BP (n = 9) or UP (n = 9) for 4 weeks, performing 6 weekly strength sessions alongside technical-tactical training. Performance outcomes included countermovement jump (CMJ), muscle power (back squat and bent-over row), and the Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT). Monitoring variables included internal load, heart rate variability (HRV), and well-being, while physiological markers included creatine kinase, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and cortisol. Data were analyzed using 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA (p < 0.05). Both groups improved SJFT performance (p < 0.01), with no between-group differences. Block planning increased lower-limb peak power (p = 0.01; d = 0.90), whereas UP showed no meaningful change. Upper-limb power and CMJ did not change in either group. Internal load showed different temporal patterns between models. Block planning presented higher HRVcv values (p = 0.04), indicating greater autonomic perturbation. Creatine kinase and TNF-α increased over time in both groups (p ≤ 0.05), while cortisol showed an interaction without clear post hoc differences. In conclusion, BP improved lower-limb power but increased physiological strain, whereas UP elicited similar judo-specific improvements with lower recovery demands. These findings highlight the importance of training organization for balancing performance and recovery in elite judo athletes.

metadata.title: Body Mass, Strength, Power, and Endurance Variations Across an Entire Season in Male Basketball Players.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: This study aimed to analyze changes in body mass, upper- and lower-boy strength, vertical jump performance, and endurance capacity in senior semiprofessional basketball players across 4 different time points (TPs) during the season. METHODS: Fifteen male basketball players (n = 15; age: 23.4 [3.4] y; height: 1.9 [0.1] m) volunteered to participate in this study. Participants were tested for body mass, 1-repetition maximum in the squat and bench press exercises, countermovement jump (CMJ) and loaded CMJ, and 30-15 intermittent fitness test. RESULTS: Significant increases were observed in absolute and relative 1-repetition maximum in the squat (P < .03; effect size [ES]: moderate to large) from TP1 to TP2, TP3, and TP4. Regarding CMJ, greater jump heights were observed at TP2 and TP4 when compared with TP3 (P < .015; ES: small). In the loaded CMJ (ES: moderate), loads were significantly greater at TP2, TP3, and TP4 compared with TP1 (P < .009; ES: moderate). Conversely, 30-15 intermittent fitness test measures showed small but nonsignificant increments (P < .086; ES: small). CONCLUSIONS: Lower-body strength and power measures improved during the preseason in male basketball players, with these athletes being able to retain strength levels across the in-season period, despite the congested competitive schedule. In contrast, CMJ performance did not change during the preseason but appeared to be negatively affected during the most competition-dense phase of the season (ie, TP3). Finally, endurance capacity and body mass remained relatively stable from the beginning of the preseason until the end of the season.

metadata.title: Beyond movement behaviours: Unravelling the prospective links between 24-hour behavioural composition and affective dynamics in adolescent athletes.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: While the full spectrum of 24-h movement behaviours - encompassing sleep (SLP), screen-based sedentary behaviour (Screen-SB), light physical activity (LPA), structured moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (S-MVPA), and unstructured moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (US-MVPA) - is consistently linked to daily affective states in adolescent athletes, existing literature has rarely examined these behaviours as an interdependent time-use composition, and largely fails to disentangle the distinct effects of structured versus unstructured MVPA subdomains on emotional outcomes. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Using a repeated-measures prospective daily design, this study included 161 adolescent athletes (101 males and 60 females). Accelerometers were used to quantify 24-h movement behaviours. Four affective dimensions were assessed through ecological momentary assessment (EMA): high-arousal positive affect, low-arousal positive affect, high-arousal negative affect, and low-arousal negative affect. Bayesian multilevel compositional models were used to estimate between- and within-person associations, while isotemporal substitution analyses evaluated the estimated effects of reallocating time between behaviours on next-day affect. RESULTS: Associations between 24-h behaviour compositions and next-day affect were more evident at the within-person level. A higher relative proportion of LPA was associated with higher high-arousal positive affect (0.305, 95% Bayesian credible interval [CrI] 0.255 to 0.354) and low-arousal positive affect (0.292, 95% CrI 0.245 to 0.338), and lower high-arousal negative affect (-0.231, 95% CrI -0.260 to -0.203) and low-arousal negative affect (-0.210, 95% CrI -0.236 to -0.185). In 30-min substitution analyses, reallocating time from other behaviours to LPA generally showed more favourable associations with next-day affect at both between- and within-person levels, although the associations varied across substitution pairs and affective dimensions. These findings highlight LPA as the behaviour most consistently associated with favourable next-day affect. CONCLUSIONS: Daily 24-h movement behaviour composition was prospectively associated with next-day affect in adolescent athletes. LPA showed the most consistent favourable associations with next-day affect, particularly when replacing SB. Promoting LPA may represent a feasible strategy for supporting affective wellbeing without adding to existing training demands.

metadata.title: Serum-derived exosomal circENC1 inhibits SMC phenotypic switching to stabilize atherosclerotic plaques by interacting with miR-513a-5p and inhibiting MYH9 degradation.
metadata.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The function of serum-derived exosomes (serum-exos) that suppress smooth muscle cell (SMC) phenotypic switching-related genes in plaque stabilization is unclear. We aimed to determine the functional role of serum-exos, which are pivotal molecular regulators, in plaque stabilization and the underlying mechanism. METHODS AND RESULTS: RNA sequencing and bioinformatic analyses of human serum-exos were used to identify circENC1, which is involved in SMC phenotypic switching and plaque stabilization. qRT-PCR assays further confirmed that the circENC1 level was substantially lower in the unstable plaque (UP)-exo group than in the stable plaque (SP)-exo group. In mice treated with serum-exos from patients with SPs, the expression of the SMC contractile phenotype indicators ACTA2 and SM22 and the plaque stability increased. In contrast, in the group treated with serum-exos from patients with UPs, CD68 expression and the vulnerability index were increased. Moreover, circENC1 expression was negatively correlated with the plaque vulnerability index in the UP-exo group and the sham group. Mechanistically, bioinformatics, chromatin isolation by RNA purification (ChIRP) and dual-luciferase reporter assays indicated that circENC1 suppressed SMC phenotypic switching by inhibiting the degradation of MYH9 and acting as a miR-513a-5p sponge to release MYOCD. CONCLUSION: Serum exosomal circENC1 inhibits SMC phenotypic switching to stabilize plaques by binding to miR-513a-5p and inhibiting MYH9 degradation, indicating that this molecule may play an important role in the clinical diagnosis and treatment of atherosclerotic plaques.

metadata.title: When Proxies Overshadow Actual Performance: Reaffirming First Principles in Applied Sport Science.
metadata.abstract: PURPOSE: In recent years, sport science has witnessed a growing emphasis on derived mechanical metrics and complex analytical approaches, often accompanied by claims that direct performance measures, such as jump height or sprint time are misleading or less informative than the proxies intended to explain them. This trend has contributed to a progressive shift away from the primary outcomes of athletic testing and toward secondary descriptors, frequently interpreted as superior indicators of performance. Using the vertical jump as a representative example, this commentary revisits fundamental foundations of classical mechanics and applied sport science to clarify the distinction between performance outcomes and mechanistic descriptors. The purpose of this commentary is to reinforce a fundamental principle of performance assessment: when the intended construct is task performance, direct outcomes, such as vertical jump height, horizontal jump distance, and sprint time should remain the primary reference. Mechanistic measures should be selected when they provide reliable and actionable information about how that outcome was achieved or why it changed. CONCLUSIONS AND PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS: Actual performance outcomes, such as jump height, jump distance, and sprint time are the most meaningful, interpretable, and relevant indicators of athletic performance. Mechanistic variables and detailed analytical approaches may provide valuable insights into underlying movement strategies and efficiency, but they should complement, rather than replace, direct performance measures. Following Occam's razor, applied sport science should continue to embrace scientific advances while avoiding the unnecessary promotion of complex, time-consuming, and expensive technologies as indispensable tools for coaches and practitioners, thereby preserving confidence in simple, valid, and accessible measures of athletic performance.

metadata.title: Psychological Profiles of Elite Cerebral Palsy Football Players: Comparison With Able-Bodied Athletes.
metadata.abstract: The purpose of this study was to examine the psychological profiles of elite cerebral palsy (CP) football players associated with athletic performance. While understanding psychological competencies is vital for high-performance para-sports, data on specific adaptive strategies remain scarce. This study compared 16 elite CP football players with 1,460 able-bodied athletes across four competitive levels (Regional-International) using the JISS-Psychological Test for Elite Athletes, which assesses 10 factors across three categories: psychological skills, self-understanding, and athletic commitment. CP players showed moderate-to-large effects in Imagination and Self-Analysis compared with athletes at all competitive levels (Hedges' g = 0.58-0.98, adjusted p < .05). These findings suggest that elite athletes with CP develop superior internal cognitive strategies to compensate for physical and environmental constraints, such as spasticity and motor uncertainty. The results highlight the importance of psychological support focused on internal simulation and self-reflection to enhance competitive excellence in para-sports.

metadata.title: The Sleep and Diet of Elite Female Australian Rules Football Athletes Differ With Age and Season Phase.
metadata.abstract: The Australian Football League Women's (AFLW) competition is comprised of a short, intensive competitive season, highlighting the importance of proper fuelling and recovery to support performance. Little is known about the dietary and sleep habits of AFLW athletes across a season, and the influence that age has on these behaviours. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the effects of season phase and age on dietary intake and sleep in elite AFLW athletes. Dietary intake and sleep were assessed in 22 AFLW athletes (25.9 ± 5.0 y) over 10 nights, including five consecutive nights during both pre-season and in-season. Dietary intake was quantified through self-reported food diaries using a smartphone application (Easy Diet Diary), and sleep via a wearable monitoring device (Oura ring). Restricted maximum likelihood mixed models were used to determine variations in dietary intake and sleep in AFLW players between season phases (i.e., pre-season vs. in-season) and age. In-season protein (115.15 ± 35.14 vs. 126.48 ± 40.10 g, p = 0.026) and fat intakes (72.93 ± 29.55 vs. 83.43 ± 33.14 g, p = 0.012) were significantly lower compared to pre-season, with no differences in sleep measures observed between season phases. While age did not influence dietary intake, each additional year of age was associated with 8 min less sleep (p = 0.001) and 4 min earlier wake times (p = 0.032). These findings suggest that protein and fat intakes fluctuate across the seasons, with increasing age being a non-modifiable risk factor for shorter sleep durations within AFLW athletes.

metadata.title: Gender Differences in Sports Injuries of the Foot and Ankle.
metadata.abstract: This article examines sex-based differences in foot and ankle injuries among female athletes, emphasizing the role of anatomic, hormonal, biomechanical, and sociocultural factors. Female athletes are disproportionately affected by ankle sprains, chronic instability, and bone stress injuries. Conditions such as relative energy deficiency in sport and the female athlete triad contribute to injury risk and long-term health consequences but remain under-recognized. This article highlights disparities in research, treatment, and outcomes, calling for improved screening, sex-specific prevention strategies, and greater inclusion of female subjects in sports medicine research to inform evidence-based care and optimize outcomes for female athletes.

metadata.title: Metabolic Bone Health in Female Patients: Focus on Foot and Ankle.
metadata.abstract: Metabolic bone health is crucial for the overall well-being of female patients. Female athletes and young females are of particular interest, as their skeletal systems are still developing and are sensitive to the hormonal and physical stress of training and diet. Stress fractures occur with higher frequency in females with risk factors such as low bone mineral density (BMD). When low bone mineral density occurs along with menstrual irregularities and relative energy deficiency, it completes the female triad (23, 27, and 28). Any discussion of female BMD and metabolic bone health must include the female triad.

metadata.title: Chitosan hydrogels: Crosslinking mechanisms, environmental adaptability, and sports-health relevance.
metadata.abstract: The development of extreme-environment sports health interfaces is shifting from short-term signal detection toward long-term interfacial service, where the reliable performance of chitosan (CS) hydrogels depends on maintaining interfacial coupling, signal transduction, and biological function under low-temperature exposure, immersion, salt-rich sweat, and dynamic wound conditions. The protonatable amino groups of CS chains serve as crosslinking sites, cationic interfacial moieties, and structural contributors to antibacterial and hemostatic activity, while hydroxyl-mediated hydration, dynamic networks, and multicomponent modification support wet adhesion, deformation recovery, and tissue repair. In winter sports, underwater and sweat-rich exercise, and sports-related wound management, the bottleneck is not a single deficiency in mechanics, conductivity, or adhesion, but coupled failure: salt-rich sweat and immersion induce charge screening, low-temperature exposure and osmotic stress disturb hydrated networks, and repeated deformation drives conductive/adhesive pathway reconstruction, leading to signal drift and impaired repair. This review summarizes chemical and physical crosslinking strategies for CS hydrogels, clarifies the roles of carbon-based materials, metal/metal-oxide nanocomponents, and natural biomacromolecules in conductive pathway formation, network reinforcement, wet interfacial regulation, and bioactive repair, and discusses environmental adaptability and sports applications. Future directions toward long-term stability, multifunctional integration, standardized evaluation, and service reliability under realistic use conditions are proposed.

metadata.title: Intermittent fasting enhances muscle regeneration via an EDA2R-NIK-myomixer axis.
metadata.abstract: Skeletal muscle exhibits a remarkable regenerative capacity that relies on adult stem cells known as satellite cells (SCs), which differentiate into myogenic progenitors to drive muscle repair. How varying energy availability alters myogenesis, however, remains unknown. Here, we demonstrate that intermittent fasting (IF) in mice upregulates a myogenic gene program, including Myomixer, a muscle-specific fusogen that facilitates the merging of progenitor cells into myofibers. IF enhances the regeneration of injured muscles by expanding the SC population and promoting the proliferation and fusion of myogenic progenitors. These effects are absent in an SC-depletion model. We show that fasting-induced EDA2R-NIK signaling increases Myomixer expression and fusion in myoblasts. Notably, mice lacking EDA2R or NIK fail to respond to the myogenic effects of IF. Furthermore, our data suggest that mice with Duchenne muscular dystrophy also benefit from an IF regimen. Therefore, IF-induced regeneration holds potential for aiding recovery from muscle damage.

metadata.title: Age-Dependent Alterations in Glutathione Metabolites Following Muscle Injury.
metadata.abstract: Age-related impairments in antioxidant defences contribute to delayed tissue repair and increased susceptibility to oxidative stress following muscle injury. Glutathione (GSH), a key cellular antioxidant, plays a central role in redox homeostasis and recovery processes. GSH is synthesized through a sequential process involving glutamic acid and cysteine, catalyzed by the rate-limiting enzyme glutamate cysteine ligase (GCL) to form γ-glutamyl cysteine (γGC), which subsequently combines with glycine to produce GSH. Using metabolomic profiling and acute skeletal muscle injury in mice, this study characterized age-dependent alterations in GSH biosynthesis. Clustering analysis identified that muscle from 12-month-old mice have a delayed GSH synthesis profile in response to injury compared to 3-month-old mice, with an age-dependent delay in γGC accumulation. This suggests that aging negatively influences metabolite profiles within the GSH synthesis pathway. As γGC lies downstream of this enzymatic step, its supplementation may bypass the GCL bottleneck. To test this, C2C12 myoblasts were treated with γGC (from 1-100 µg/mL), however this did not affect myoblast proliferation or differentiation. These data suggest detrimental age-related dysregulation of GSH-related metabolites in skeletal muscle repair, particularly γGC, however further examination of the role of exogenous γGC supplementation in this process is required to identify further therapeutic benefit.

metadata.title: Growth factor printing into fusing cell spheroids to engineer spatially complex tissues.
metadata.abstract: Cell spheroids are powerful building blocks for tissue engineering. To create spatially heterogeneous, native-like tissues, typically individual stem/progenitor cell-derived spheroids are primed toward specific phenotypes prior to assembly into larger tissues. However, this pre-specification impairs spheroid fusion into scaled-up, cohesive tissues due to secretion of boundary proteins around individual spheroid peripheries over time. In this study, we report a bioprinting platform for spatially patterning growth factors into an immature living matrix of spheroids to locally direct cell fate in situ. Laponite-containing bioinks supported sustained delivery of transforming growth factor-beta 3 (TGF-β3) into a bath of immature mesenchymal stromal cell-derived spheroids, resulting in superior chondrogenesis compared to standard media supplementation. When TGF-β3 and bone morphogenetic protein 2 were patterned into an initially phenotypically homogeneous living tissue matrix, an osteochondral-like gradient developed over time in culture. This bioprinting platform enables spatially complex tissue engineering with potential applications in musculoskeletal tissues and beyond.

metadata.title: Analytical strategies for distinguishing endogenous and exogenous anabolic androgenic steroids in doping control.
metadata.abstract: Doping control for anabolic androgenic steroids (AASs) must separate endogenous physiology from exogenous administration when the same molecular entities occur on both sides of the boundary. This Critical Review evaluates analytical strategies for that source-attribution problem, with emphasis on urinary steroid profiling, longitudinal interpretation, compound-specific isotope ratio mass spectrometry, intact phase-II metabolites, alternative matrices, high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS), and data-driven evidence integration. Current practice relies on a staged logic: routine steroid-profile measurements define marker behavior, the steroidal module of the Athlete Biological Passport (ABP) evaluates individual changes, and gas chromatography-combustion-isotope ratio mass spectrometry (GC-C-IRMS) supplies orthogonal source evidence when pseudo-endogenous steroids or atypical profiles require confirmation. UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 2B17 (UGT2B17) deletion, sex, menstrual-cycle phase, pregnancy, medication, and sample degradation can alter marker concentrations and ratios. Intact conjugates, dried blood spots (DBS), HRMS metabolite discovery, and statistical tools can provide additional evidence, but their performance depends on validation for the relevant matrix and administration scenario. The most defensible strategy is therefore a tiered framework that combines longitudinal interpretation, source-specific chemical evidence, and expert review.

metadata.abstract: This document outlines recommendations for managing competitive athletes with arrhythmias and risks of sudden cardiac arrest, emphasizing individualized risk assessment, shared decision-making, and return-to-play protocols tailored to each athlete's cardiac profile and sport demands. It provides evaluation strategies for ventricular arrhythmias, implantable cardiac defibrillators, atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia, Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern/syndrome, and syncope, alongside guidance for electrocardiogram interpretation in athletes. A key focus is placed on differentiating between low-risk and high-risk conditions, with recommendations for treatment strategies and ongoing monitoring to ensure athletes' safety.

metadata.title: Running the Numbers: High Metabolic Load Distance as an Alternative to Traditional External Load Metrics in Elite Women's Football.
metadata.abstract: This study examined the relationship between High Metabolic Load Distance (HMLD) and both session RPE (sRPE) and athlete wellness in women's football and compared it with traditional load monitoring metrics. An observational design was used to collect data from one elite women's football team during training and games in the 2024/25 A-League W season. Twenty-four athletes wore global positioning devices to capture external load metrics, including total distance (TD), high-speed running distance (HSRD) and HMLD. Session RPE and daily wellness were collected through online questionnaires. Generalised additive models were used to examine non-linear relationships between external load, subsequent days' wellness and RPE, and relationships between morning wellness and same-day external load. Higher load was associated with increased sRPE, and poorer next-day wellness, with effects diminishing within two to 3 days post-session. Across all outcomes, HMLD demonstrated stronger and more consistent relationships than TD and HSRD, explaining a greater proportion of variance in wellness and sRPE. Same-day wellness was associated with differences in distances, with higher motivation and lower fatigue corresponding to higher HMLD. HMLD demonstrated comparatively stronger associations with immediate perceived exertion and short-term athlete reported wellness than traditional distance-based metrics in this cohort. These findings support the application of HMLD as a practical and sensitive measure to inform training decision-making in elite women's football.

metadata.title: Shoulder Arthritis.
metadata.abstract: Glenohumeral osteoarthritis is a common, debilitating joint disease characterized by progressive cartilage loss, subchondral bone remodeling, and capsular stiffness, leading to pain, restricted motion, and functional impairment. Diagnosis relies on both clinical evaluation and imaging studies. Classification systems, such as the Walch classification, assist in assessing disease severity and guiding treatment decisions. Management begins with conservative approaches, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), physical therapy, and intra-articular injections, progressing to surgical interventions such as total or reverse shoulder arthroplasty for advanced disease. Early diagnosis and patient-specific treatment are essential to ensuring optimal patient outcomes.

metadata.title: Gingival mesenchymal stem cells attenuate high glucose-induced gingival fibroblast damage and ferroptosis by upregulating ALDH2.
metadata.abstract: Periodontitis is a multifactorial inflammatory disease that results in the loss of periodontal supporting tissues, which is closely associated with diabetes. Moreover, gingival mesenchymal stem cells (GMSCs) have been identified as a newer source for periodontal tissue reconstruction/regeneration. It has been reported that aldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (ALDH2) could alleviate inflammation and promote osteogenic differentiation of periodontal ligament stem cells in periodontitis by blocking ferroptosis. However, the role of ALDH2 and GMSCs in periodontitis is poorly defined. Transcriptomic data from the periodontitis GSE10334 dataset were used for WGCNA analysis. Hub genes were identified using key modules from WGCNA and ferroptosis-related genes and type 2 diabetes mellitus-associated genes from GeneCards dataset. A periodontitis cell model in vitro was established by high glucose (HG) treatment in human gingival fibroblasts (HGFs). Gene expression was detected using real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) and western blot. Cell viability, proliferation, and migration were detected by Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8), 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU), and Transwell assays. Interleukin-1β (IL-1β), IL-6, IL-8, and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP1) were determined using ELISA. Lipid reactive oxygen species (ROS), glutathione (GSH), and Fe2+ levels were measured using commercial kits. The gingival mesenchymal stem cell (GMSC) morphology and characteristics were identified. GMSCs were co-cultured with HG-induced HGFs in Transwell system to analyze the effect of ALDH2 in GMSCs on HG-induced HGF damage. Herein, integrated bioinformatics analyses (WGCNA on GSE10334 dataset combined with ferroptosis- and type 2 diabetes mellitus-related genes from GeneCards) were applied to identify ALDH2 as a candidate gene. Then, the role and the therapeutic potential of ALDH2-modified GMSCs were investigated in HG-induced HGF injury in vitro. ALDH2 expression was decreased in HG-treated HGFs (P < 0.05), and its overexpression reversed HG-induced HGF cell proliferation and migration inhibition, and inflammation and ferroptosis promotion (P < 0.05). In co-cultured systems, ALDH2 upregulation in GMSCs relieved HG-treated HGF dysfunction and ferroptosis (P < 0.05). GMSCs could protect HGFs from HG-induced dysfunction, inflammatory response, and ferroptosis through upregulating ALDH2, suggesting a potential protective mechanism that may inform future therapeutic strategies for diabetic periodontitis, pending validation in more physiologically relevant models.

metadata.title: 660 nm LED preconditioning programs mitochondrial signaling in BMSCs for functional tracheal cartilage regeneration.
metadata.abstract: Stem-cell-based cartilage regeneration is limited not only by cell delivery, but also by the difficulty of establishing a stable and functionally competent regenerative cell state before implantation. Here, we report a photonic mitochondrial programming strategy in which 660 nm light-emitting diode (LED) irradiation preconditions bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) to enhance functional tracheal cartilage regeneration. BMSCs were seeded onto egg white-derived ring-shaped porous scaffolds and exposed to defined 660 nm LED irradiation before implantation. Among the tested irradiation conditions, 15 J/cm2 optimally promoted BMSC proliferation, chondrogenic differentiation and cartilage-like extracellular matrix deposition, while suppressing fibrotic, hypertrophic and matrix-degrading phenotypes. Mechanistically, 660 nm LED irradiation enhanced cytochrome c oxidase (CCO) activity, mitochondrial membrane potential, adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production and respiratory function, accompanied by moderate reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling. This mitochondrial bioenergetic-redox response activated the PI3K/Akt/mTOR/GSK3β-SOX9 axis, thereby promoting type II collagen, aggrecan and glycosaminoglycan-rich matrix formation. Pharmacological inhibition of ROS signaling, mitochondrial activity, PI3K or mTOR attenuated the LED-induced chondrogenic program. In a rabbit tracheal cartilage ring defect model, 15 J/cm2-preconditioned BMSC-scaffold constructs improved cartilage-like tissue formation, airway epithelial repair, lumen patency and mechanical support after 30 days of observation. These findings support 660 nm LED irradiation as a controllable mitochondrial preconditioning strategy for stem-cell-based functional cartilage regeneration.

metadata.title: Clonal articular cartilage progenitors outperform mesenchymal stromal cells in mitigating post-traumatic osteoarthritis.
metadata.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to compare the functional, pathological, and immunomodulatory properties of articular chondroprogenitors (ACPs) with those of bone-marrow-derived mesenchymal stromal cells (MSCs) in preventing the progression of post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA) after destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM) injury in a mouse model. METHOD: ACP and MSC were isolated from three horses and assessed for their immunomodulatory capacity in vitro. Aliquots of selected ACP clones and MSCs were injected intra-articularly into male mice 1-week post destabilization of the medial meniscus (DMM). The functional mobility of the mice before the injury and at weeks 2, 4, and 8 post-injury was assessed by two methods: ANY-maze™ voluntary mobility monitoring and DigiGait™ compulsory gait analysis. Upon euthanasia, joints were collected for histological scoring. RESULTS: In vitro assessments demonstrated that ACPs and MSCs had anti-inflammatory properties: both treatments produced lower levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines, while only the ACPs produced more anti-inflammatory cytokines than controls. In vivo, both ACPs and MSCs lessened the effects of DMM on mobility. Histological scoring revealed significant reductions of PTOA in the medial compartment with ACPs relative to both MSCs and vehicle controls. Overall, ACPs effectively reduced PTOA progression to a greater extent than MSCs. CONCLUSION: Our findings demonstrated that both equine ACP and MSC treatments provided symptom modification over vehicle controls in a short-term animal study. Notably, ACPs may be more efficacious than MSCs at reducing structural joint pathology.

metadata.title: EMSCs-derived exosomes rescue p75NTR-/- -mediated osteogenesis deficiency via PI3K/Akt/ERK1/2 signaling pathways.
metadata.abstract: The repair of the critical-sized bone defects remains a major challenge for orthopedic surgeons, particularly when osteogenesis is impaired by p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75NTR) deficiency. However, the underlying molecular mechanisms are not fully understood. This study aimed to clarify the role of p75NTR in bone regeneration and to develop a cell-free approach to rescue p75NTR-/- deficiency-mediated osteogenic deficiency through a controlled releasing of wild-type ectomesenchymal stem cells exosomes (WT-Exo) which were incorporated into silk fibroin/polycaprolactone2:5/polyvinyl alcohol (SF/PCL2:5/PVA) coaxial nanofibrous membranes. p75NTR-/- mice exhibited a reduced bone mass and delayed ossification, while WT-Exo-loaded membranes partially restored osteogenic deficiency in p75NTR-/- cells and enhanced expression of osteogenic markers such as alkaline phosphatase (ALP), collagen type I (Col-I), osteopontin (OPN) and runt-related transcription factor 2 (Runx2) aaccompanied by activating of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (Akt)/extracellular signal-regulated kinase 1/2 (ERK1/2) signaling pathway. Following implantation of the WT-Exo-loaded membranes into the critical-sized cranial defects in p75NTR-/- mice, new bone formation in the defect site was significantly improved by a sustained release of WT-Exo. Overall, the findings in this study highlighted the critical role of p75NTR in osteogenic differentiation of ectomesenchymal stem cells (EMSCs) and demonstrated that WT-Exo, delivered via the coaxial electrospun membranes, represented an effective cell-free intervention method to reverse bone formation deficiency caused by p75NTR deficiency, providing a promising strategy for gene deficiency-related bone diseases.

metadata.title: Advancing regenerative biomaterials and translational strategies in orthopaedic traumatology.
metadata.abstract: The 2025 Orthopaedic Trauma Association's Basic Science Focus Forum featured a symposium on regenerative biomaterials and translational strategies for orthopaedic trauma. Four experts presented complementary perspectives on the next generation of bone and soft tissue repair: Dr. J. Tracy Watson described how orthobiologics and refined spacer design can be used to engineer a better Masquelet induced membrane; Dr. Lauren Priddy presented evidence that hydroxyapatite coatings can mitigate the rapid degradation of additively manufactured magnesium scaffolds; Dr. Vaida Glatt described the development and clinical translation of the Biomimetic Hematoma scaffold for bone and muscle regeneration; and Dr. Katherine Hixon outlined how the 3R principles (Replacement, Reduction, Refinement) can serve as a framework to accelerate musculoskeletal regenerative engineering. Collectively, the symposium underscored a shift toward biologically informed, clinically predictive, and ethically responsible engineering solutions for the patients who sustain musculoskeletal trauma.

metadata.title: Gene amplification during differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells towards chondrocytes.
metadata.abstract: For decades, gene amplification was described as an attribute of tumor cells and as a physiological mechanism to increase gene copy numbers for the higher protein demand during the development of amphibians and flies. Notably, gene amplification has since been detected in normal mammalian cells during differentiation. Numerous amplified genes detected in tumor cells overlap with amplified genes detected during stem cell differentiation. Since stem cells have a valuable potency in regenerative therapies and since cartilage regeneration is a highly demanded therapeutic strategy, the current study investigated gene amplification dynamics during the chondrogenic differentiation of human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs). Using quantitative PCR, copy number changes were analyzed for genes previously implicated in differentiation, as well as genes amplified in chondrosarcoma, including CDK4, MDM2, AGAP2, CPT1B, SHANK3, TRIB1 and MYC. Amplifications were transient and stage-specific: CDK4, CPT1B and SHANK3 exhibited the highest copy number increases at day 2, followed by a gradual decline by day 7, whereas AGAP2 and MDM2 increased later in differentiation. Laser microdissection of toluidine blue-stained areas revealed heterogeneity in amplification patterns: CDK4 amplification was prominent in areas lacking or showing moderate proteoglycan deposition; CPT1B amplification occurred in regions with absent, moderate or intense proteoglycan deposition; and SHANK3 amplification was restricted to areas with intense proteoglycan deposition. Notably, regions with the strongest proteoglycan staining exhibited no gene amplification, suggesting that gene amplification is an early, transient event that diminishes as differentiation progresses. These findings highlight gene amplification as a mechanism during chondrogenesis, potentially critical for early differentiation stages and genome stability in mature cells.

metadata.title: PTHrP suppresses BMP2-induced osteochondral differentiation and preserves cartilage phenotype in mesenchymal stem cells via inactivating PI3K-AKT signaling.
metadata.abstract: Bone morphogenetic protein 2 (BMP2) has the potential to drive multipotent mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) to undergo chondral-osteogenic (including hypertrophic chondrocyte) differentiation. Parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) plays an essential role in fetal endochondral ossification, although persistent PTHrP stimulation leads to postnatal bone loss. Here, we investigated the effects of PTHrP on BMP2-induced endochondral ossification through hypertrophic chondrocyte differentiation of MSCs. We found that silencing PTHrP expression inhibited BMP2-induced chondrogenic, hypertrophic, and osteogenic differentiation of MSCs, while overexpression of PTHrP promoted BMP2-induced chondrogenic differentiation of MSCs and suppressed BMP2-induced hypertrophic differentiation of MSCs. Using stem cell implantation studies in athymic nude mice, we demonstrated that while MSCs with silenced PTHrP expression exhibited significantly reduced endochondral ossification of subcutaneous cartilage, overexpression of PTHrP promoted the growth of subcutaneous cartilage while significantly delaying ossification, leading to the preservation of cartilage phenotype. Mechanistically, we showed that exogenous PTHrP promoted BMP2-induced chondrogenic differentiation of MSCs by up-regulating Sox9 expression and inactivating PI3K-AKT signaling. Collectively, our findings strongly suggest that PTHrP may play an important role in mediating BMP2-induced chondral-osteogenic differentiation of MSCs by inactivating PI3K-AKT signaling, indicating that PTHrP may be exploited for endochondral cartilage-bone tissue engineering.

metadata.title: Ultrasound-triggered bio-scaffold integrating engineered stem cells for cartilage regeneration.
metadata.abstract: Articular cartilage repair remains a major clinical challenge due to the limited regenerative capacity of the tissue and the poor therapeutic efficacy of current treatments. Although stem cell-based therapies hold promise, their clinical outcomes are often compromised by insufficient chondrogenic differentiation, phenotypic instability, and rapid cell loss in the dynamic joint environment. Herein, we report an ultrasound-responsive, bio-scaffold system (e-BMSCs/Gel) designed to enhance cartilage regeneration through coordinated biochemical and genetic regulation. In this system, bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) are engineered by internalizing nanobubbles (NBs) loaded with TGF-β3 protein and CRISPR/Cas9 plasmids targeting the YAP (pCas9-YAP), termed T@NBspDNA. Additionally, to enhance cell retention and survival, engineered BMSCs (e-BMSCs) are encapsulated within a thermosensitive thiolated-chitosan/hydroxyapatite hydrogel that rapidly forms in situ. Under US stimulation, the synchronized activation of TGF-β3 release and YAP gene silencing significantly promoted the chondrogenic differentiation of e-BMSCs. Furthermore, in vivo evaluation in a rat articular cartilage defect model demonstrates that US-activated e-BMSCs/Gel effectively promotes hyaline-like cartilage regeneration and improves structural restoration of the defect site. Overall, this work presents a controllable bio-scaffold platform, offering a novel strategy for effective cartilage regeneration.

metadata.title: Targeting the lactate/P300/H3K18la epigenetic pathway with a mechanoadaptive biomimetic hydrogel to suppress traumatic tendon heterotopic ossification.
metadata.abstract: Traumatic heterotopic ossification (HO) is a debilitating complication of tendon injury, yet its pathogenic mechanisms remain elusive and effective preventive strategies are lacking. Here, we identify a glycometabolic-epigenetic axis that drives HO progression. Single-cell profiling and functional analyses reveal that hypoxic chondrocytes undergo glycolytic reprogramming, leading to lactate accumulation and transfer into tendon-derived mesenchymal stem cells (TD-MSCs) through MCT1. This metabolic coupling promotes P300-dependent histone H3 lysine 18 lactylation (H3K18la), activating osteogenic programs characterized by Col6a1, Zhx3, Lox and Vdr expression and thereby facilitating pathological endochondral ossification. Guided by this mechanism, we develop a tendon-adhesive hydrogel (GelHA-A485@Exos) that integrates mechanical repair with targeted epigenetic modulation. MSC-derived exosomes enable localized delivery of the P300 inhibitor A485, suppressing H3K18la and aberrant osteogenic activation, while the hydrogel scaffold enhances tendon regeneration. In vivo and in vitro studies demonstrate that GelHA-A485@Exos promotes tendon healing while preventing HO formation. Our findings establish metabolic-epigenetic communication as a central regulator of traumatic HO and provide a translational therapeutic strategy for its clinical prevention.

metadata.title: Creating Consensus: Establishing a Definition of Sports Pharmacy and Its Emerging Role in Sports Medicine.
metadata.abstract: Sports pharmacy has become an increasingly recognized specialty within the broader pharmacy profession and serves as a complementary discipline to sport medicine. Yet, the field has lacked a formally established, internationally accepted definition. The absence of standardized terminology has hindered academic integration, interprofessional collaboration, and policy development. This work aimed to establish the first consensus-derived definition of sports pharmacy, accompanied by a responsibility statement to guide future education, certification, and research. In 2024, the US Sports Pharmacy Group (USSPG), comprising pharmacists, academics, anti-doping professionals, student pharmacists, and competitive athletes from diverse US states and international settings, convened a discrete subgroup, the Define Sports Pharmacy Taskforce, to lead the development of a formal definition of sports pharmacy. The taskforce conducted a thematic analysis of existing literature and reviewed 123 open-ended member responses collected between 2022 and 2024. Eight recurring practice themes emerged and informed iterative drafting cycles. Draft definitions were subsequently reviewed by interprofessional stakeholders, including physicians, elite athletes, and anti-doping practitioners. The resulting definition emphasizes medication management, anti-doping advocacy, interprofessional collaboration, athlete-centered ethical care, and the use of therapeutic and pharmacological strategies to optimize performance, support recovery, and protect sports integrity across all levels of physical activity. This consensus-derived framework provides standardized terminology to support the development of educational pathways, establish certification standards, and promote the integration of pharmacists into athlete support teams.

metadata.title: Longitudinal association between vertical jump performance and sprint acceleration performance in sprinters.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: This study aimed at investigating the associations between changes in sprint performance and changes in vertical jump performances and to clarify whether the vertical jump performances would reflect better sprint acceleration performance. METHODS: To examine the association between changes in sprint performance and vertical jump performance, two experimental sessions per participant were conducted using an identical protocol with a one- or two-month interval. Seventeen male sprinters performed a 60-m sprint and 3 vertical jump tests in each test session. RESULTS: The change in 60-m sprint time was correlated with changes in countermovement jump (CMJ) height (r=-0.573) and ankle continuous rebound jump (AJ) contact time (r=0.660). Changes in sprint acceleration were correlated with changes in squat jump (SJ) height from the 10th to 16th steps (r=0.495-0.676), with changes in CMJ height from the 13th to 16th steps (r=0.509-0.587), with changes in AJ height from the 15th to 19th steps (r=0.493-0.583), with changes in AJ contact time from the 8th to 14th steps (r=-0.499 to -0.570), and with changes in AJ index from the 15th to 19th steps (r=0.496-0.627). CONCLUSIONS: The SJ and CMJ heights, as well as AJ contact time, may likely be indicators of better sprint acceleration performance during the middle acceleration section, while AJ height and index are likely useful for indirectly assessing sprint acceleration performance during the final acceleration section. Sprinters and coaches can use these vertical jumps for monitoring changes in sprint performance for the entire distance and specific acceleration sections.

metadata.title: Osteoarthritis-Microenvironment-Triggered Phase Alteration of Injectable Conductive Hydrogel for Attenuating Cartilage Degradation.
metadata.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is associated with excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, which contributes substantially to chondrocyte dysfunction, oxidative stress, and cartilage degradation. Although stimuli-responsive hydrogels have emerged as promising platforms for OA therapy, conventional hydrogel-based systems exhibit limited sensitivity and require external detection equipment, highlighting the need for a simple, sensitive, and directly observable monitoring system. To address these challenges, we developed a ROS-triggered, in situ-forming gel-sol transition of a polydopamine (PDA)-loaded, diselenide-crosslinked polymer dot (PD) injectable hydrogel (HGC-PDA@PD or OA gel) as a monitorable theranostic for OA therapy at physiological temperature (37°C). The monitorable OA microenvironment-responsive hydrogel relied on interactions between the high ROS levels in OA cartilage and the OA gel, which triggered diselenide bond cleavage and the release of PDA from PD, causing a unique gel-sol transition of the OA gel. Owing to PDA release after diselenide breakage, the fluorescence and electroconductivity of the OA gel changed, which could serve as additional signals during OA detection. In vitro studies demonstrated the sensitive gel-sol transition of OA gel towards OA-induced immature articular chondrocytes (IL-1β/siSOD1/siCatalase-transfected iMACs). Furthermore, the OA gel showed a distinct gel-sol transition in cartilage of an in vivo OA mouse model compared with that in control mice. The lower transcription levels of cartilage matrix-degrading enzymes (ADAMTS4, ADAMTS5, MMP-3, and MMP-13) observed after OA gel injection confirmed that the OA gel could scavenge ROS and attenuate cartilage damage, revealing its potential application for dual-function OA diagnosis and rehabilitation.

metadata.title: Evaluation of a four-herb Chinese medicine formula at different concentrations on muscle damage and inflammation in a rat model of DOMS.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) impairs exercise recovery, while current treatments remain limited. Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) formulas may provide safe, multi-target interventions. OBJECTIVES: This study evaluated the dose-dependent protective effects of a four-herb Chinese medicine formulation (safflower, Chinese Angelica, peach kernel and myrrh) against DOMS in a rat model. METHODS: Thirty-two male SPF SD rats were randomly allocated to control or low- (1696 mg/kg), medium- (3392 mg/kg), or high-dose (6784 mg/kg) groups. The formulation was administered orally for 11 days, with DOMS induced by exhaustive swimming on day 8. Serum CK, Mb, CRP, IL-6, and PGE2 were measured at baseline and at 24, 48, 72, and 96 h post-exercise. RESULTS: The medium- and high-dose groups exhibited significantly lower serum CK, Mb, CRP, IL-6, and PGE2 levels than controls, with the high-dose group showing the largest reductions. The low-dose group showed limited or no significant reductions in most markers, demonstrating a clear dose-dependent protective effect. CONCLUSIONS: The formulation dose-dependently attenuates muscle damage and inflammation in a rat DOMS model, with high-dose treatment achieving the fastest recovery. Clinical trials are warranted to confirm the efficacy and safety in humans.

metadata.title: GW9508 suppresses chondrogenic differentiation of BMSCs and attenuates heterotopic ossification without significantly affecting osteogenic differentiation.
metadata.abstract: Post-traumatic heterotopic ossification (HO) is a pathological bone-forming disorder characterized by aberrant activation of bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) and ectopic endochondral ossification; however, effective targeted therapies remain limited. This study investigated the regulatory effects and underlying mechanisms of GW9508, an agonist of free fatty acid receptors GPR40/120, on HO progression. After determining the safe concentration range of GW9508 using a CCK-8 assay, in vitro chondrogenic and osteogenic differentiation models were established to evaluate its effects on BMSC lineage commitment through qRT-PCR, Western blotting, and histological staining. A C57BL/6 mouse Achilles tendon transection model was further used to assess in vivo efficacy by micro-computed tomography, histological analysis, and immunofluorescence staining. GW9508 did not affect BMSC proliferation but significantly reduced the expression of chondrogenic markers Sox9, Col2a1, and Acan at both mRNA and protein levels in a dose-dependent manner, accompanied by decreased cartilage extracellular matrix deposition. In contrast, GW9508 showed no significant effects on osteogenic markers Runx2, ALP, and Sp7 or mineralized nodule formation. In vivo, local administration of GW9508 reduced ectopic bone formation and inhibited both early chondrogenesis and subsequent ossification. Collectively, these findings suggest that GW9508 attenuates HO progression by suppressing the chondrogenic differentiation of BMSCs, thereby limiting the subsequent endochondral ossification process. Under the present in vitro experimental conditions, GW9508 selectively inhibited chondrogenic differentiation without causing significant alterations in osteogenic differentiation. These findings provide new insights into potential therapeutic strategies for post-traumatic HO.

metadata.title: DNA-adsorbing nanozyme hydrogel reprograms the immuno-oxidative microenvironment to support stem cell-based cartilage repair in osteoarthritis.
metadata.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a prevalent degenerative joint disease, and stem cell therapy is often limited by a hostile joint microenvironment. Excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) and damage-associated cell-free DNA (cfDNA) cooperatively drive innate immune activation, inflammatory macrophage polarization, and chondrogenic instability, forming an immuno-oxidative barrier to cartilage repair. Here, we developed a bioactive DNA-adsorbing nanozyme hydrogel (MNKB/HA) to remodel this niche and enhance BMSC-mediated cartilage repair. MNKB/HA integrates Mn3O4 nanozymes with Kartogenin (KGN)-engineered bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) in an injectable hyaluronic acid matrix. Mn3O4 exhibited SOD- and CAT-like activities, scavenging O2·-, H2O2, and ·OH, while efficiently adsorbing cfDNA and CpG-ODN to suppress TLR9/MyD88 signaling and M1 polarization and promote M2 polarization. In vitro, 10 μg/mL Mn3O4 was cytocompatible, protected BMSCs and chondrocytes from H2O2-induced apoptosis, and reshaped inflammatory secretion, with IL-10 increased 8.3-fold and TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β reduced. KGN stabilized the chondrogenic phenotype (SOX9, COL Ⅱ, ACAN), while its combination with Mn3O4 synergistically enhanced chondrogenic stability under oxidative/inflammatory stress. In rat OA, intra-articular MNKB/HA reduced OARSI scores, restored COL II and ACAN, decreased MMP13, improved subchondral bone microarchitecture, and attenuated synovitis and osteophytes. MNKB/HA also reduced synovial cfDNA, weakened TLR9 signaling, promoted M2 polarization, and showed intra-articular retention for at least 10 days without notable systemic toxicity. Thus, MNKB/HA remodels the immuno-oxidative niche through synergistic ROS scavenging and cfDNA adsorption, providing a strategy for stem cell-mediated cartilage repair in OA.

metadata.title: An equine bone marrow aspirate concentrate protocol yields a predictable cellular and cytokine profile.
metadata.abstract: BACKGROUND: Bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC) is a quick, minimally invasive, point-of-care therapy for equine orthopaedic injuries. Despite growing clinical use, standardised manufacturing methods are lacking, and the final product remains poorly characterised. OBJECTIVE: To develop a reproducible protocol for equine BMAC production that yields predictable cellular and cytokine compositions. STUDY DESIGN: In vitro analytical study. METHODS: Bone marrow aspirate (BMA) was harvested from the sternum of eight healthy adult horses and filtered to remove possible bony spicules. After centrifugation at 1000 × g for 10 min, the buffy coat was collected to generate BMAC. Cellular composition was assessed using standard haematology and cytology, and cytokine concentrations were measured using commercially available enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation. RESULTS: BMA filtration successfully removed potential bony material without significantly altering the cellular profile. Cells were predictably concentrated in BMAC: total nucleated cells increased from 77 ± 30 × 103/μL to 240 ± 57 × 103/μL; and platelets from 119 ± 34 × 103/μL to 269 ± 81 × 103/μL. Anti-inflammatory cytokines were increased in BMAC: IL-1ra increased from 18,611.3 ± 5509.1 to 36,598.8 ± 5971.8 pg/mL; IL-10 from 9.0 ± 7.5 to 19.1 ± 15.6 ng/mL; and TGF-β1 from 2535.0 ± 3018.7 to 5073.8 ± 2175.9 pg/mL. Of the pro-inflammatory cytokines measured, only IL-1β was increased (287.5 ± 22.5 to 475.1 ± 206.0 pg/mL), while TNF-α and IL-6 were unchanged. MAIN LIMITATIONS: The small cohort size (n = 8) limited sensitivity for detecting minor effects. The cytokine panel, while representative, does not encompass all potential bioactive mediators, and single-time-point measurements do not necessarily reflect in vivo release kinetics. The clinical efficacy of BMAC was not evaluated, preventing direct correlation between compositional features and therapeutic outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: The BMAC protocol yielded consistently concentrated nucleated cells, preserved cellular morphology, and enhanced the anti-inflammatory cytokine profile relative to post-filtration BMA. These findings provide a biological rationale for intra-articular and intra-lesional use of BMAC in equine patients.

metadata.title: Adhesive hydrogel-mediated spatiotemporal delivery of garlic-derived nanovesicles reprograms immunometabolism to rescue periodontal bone regeneration.
metadata.abstract: The core challenge in regenerating inflammatory bone defects, such as periodontitis-related bone resorption, lies in the dysregulation of the immune-metabolic microenvironment, which required implanted materials to simultaneously possess tissue sealing properties, sustained immune modulation capacity and metabolic intervention functions. Herein, garlic-derived exosome-like nanovesicles (GaELNs), exhibiting anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory activities, are embedded in an injectable, tissue-adhesive polyethylene glycol hydrogel (GaE-PEG) to meet the challenges. The hydrogel exhibited favorable tissue adhesion and sustained release of GaELN-associated protein in vitro. GaE-PEG promoted macrophage polarization toward an anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine expression. In lipopolysaccharide-stimulated periodontal ligament stem cells, GaE-PEG alleviated mitochondrial oxidative stress, restored oxidative phosphorylation, suppressed excessive glycolysis, and enhanced osteogenic differentiation. Transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses linked these effects to mitochondrial metabolic regulation, while oligomycin treatment attenuated the osteogenic response, supporting a contribution of oxidative phosphorylation. In a rat model of periodontitis-related bone defects, GaE-PEG reduced local inflammation and promoted alveolar bone regeneration, with improved regenerative outcomes compared with a single local injection of free GaELNs at an equivalent dose and Bio-Gide™/Bio-Oss™ treatment. These findings support an adhesive hydrogel strategy integrating local nanovesicle delivery with immunomodulation and metabolic regulation to promote bone regeneration under inflammatory conditions.
